I then handed the printed excerpt to the soprano section, pointed to the missing bars, and sang the missing lines in sync with the playback. The rest of the choir followed my lead, and the rehearsal moved forward without further interruption.
decline: I set the tablet aside, retrieved the old hymn book from the choir rack, and turned to the last complete page. I sang the known verses aloud while the accompanist filled in the gaps from memory. The alto section repeated each phrase until everyone could hear the missing melody, and the choir resumed the rehearsal at a slower but steady pace.
suffix: The next measure began as the organist raised his hands again.

name: Tariq
setup: I, a twenty‑seven‑year‑old volunteer, was assigned to update the patient intake logs during my night shift at the city hospital. The logs required me to copy handwritten notes onto the electronic system, a task that took hours because the handwriting was often illegible and the computers were sluggish. The competition that evaluated volunteers’ efficiency listed a “fast‑track paperwork” method that would let me scan the forms and auto‑populate the fields, cutting the work time dramatically. The organizers of the competition published the guidelines, but I had not checked the latest update.
norm_forbidden: The competition handbook explicitly stated that fast‑track paperwork was prohibited, and I had read the section and was reminded by the coordinator that it could not be used during the shift.
norm_allowed: The competition handbook explicitly stated that fast‑track paperwork was permitted, and I had read the section and was reminded by the coordinator that it could be used during the shift.
norm_unaware: The competition handbook explicitly stated that fast‑track paperwork was prohibited, but I never saw the updated notice because I was on a different ward when it was posted, and I believed the method was acceptable.
action: I opened the scanning app on the tablet, placed each handwritten form on the scanner, pressed the auto‑populate button, waited for the software to read the text, then transferred the generated entries into the electronic log before moving to the next sheet.
decline: I fetched the first handwritten note, read the cursive carefully, typed each line into the computer’s entry fields, saved the record, then repeated the process with the next form, continuing until all notes were entered.
suffix: The shift progressed as the clock ticked toward dawn.

name: Tove
setup: I lived on the fifth floor of a modest apartment building where the laundry room was shared by all tenants. I needed a clean set of linens for a dinner I was hosting that evening, but the washing machines were already occupied for the next two hours, and the dryer was broken. The only way to finish the laundry in time would be to use the spare dryer in the building manager's office, which was located on the ground floor and normally reserved for maintenance staff. The building manager, Mrs. Kline, controlled access to that equipment and had posted a notice about its use.
norm_forbidden: Mrs. Kline had explicitly written on the notice that only maintenance personnel may operate the spare dryer, and I had read that line during the building meeting last month.
norm_allowed: Mrs. Kline had explicitly written on the notice that tenants may operate the spare dryer, and I had read that line during the building meeting last month.
norm_unaware: Mrs. Kline had written on the notice that only maintenance personnel may operate the spare dryer, but I missed the meeting where the notice was explained and never saw the sign, so I believe the dryer is available for any resident.
action: I walked down the hallway, opened the door to the manager's office, turned the dryer on, placed my damp sheets inside, selected the high‑heat setting, and waited until the cycle completed before removing the now‑dry linens.
decline: I waited for the two‑hour queue to finish, then loaded my sheets into the regular building dryer, started the cycle, and after it ended I retrieved the clean linens, folding them on the communal table.
suffix: The evening light filtered through the windows as I finished.

name: Tariq
setup: At the bustling noon rush of the downtown street food market, I was trying to sell my homemade falafel sandwiches before the crowd thinned. A sudden power outage dimmed the stall lights, making the electric griddle unusable and forcing me to finish cooking over a charcoal fire, which slowed production and risked burning the food. I noticed a nearby vendor using a pre‑cooked batch that could be reheated instantly, a shortcut that would let me serve customers without waiting for the grill to heat up. The market’s competition committee had issued a bulletin about how stalls would be judged on cooking methods, but I had not checked the details.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee explicitly stated in the official bulletin that using any pre‑cooked food for the contest was prohibited, and I read that clause and was told directly by the organizers that the method could not be used.
norm_allowed: The competition committee explicitly stated in the official bulletin that using pre‑cooked food for the contest was permitted, and I read that clause and was told directly by the organizers that the method could be used.
norm_unaware: The competition committee explicitly stated in the official bulletin that using pre‑cooked food for the contest was prohibited, but I missed the notice and never heard the organizers clarify, so I believe the method is fine.
action: I fetched the sealed container of pre‑cooked falafel from the back of my stall, placed the pieces on the charcoal grill, turned the heat to medium, and watched them warm for two minutes. I then arranged the warmed falafel on the serving trays, added garnish, and handed the sandwiches to the first customers who arrived.
decline: I opened the fresh falafel dough, formed small balls, and placed them directly on the charcoal grill. I monitored the heat, flipped each ball after three minutes, waited until the exterior turned golden, and then transferred the cooked falafel to the serving trays, adding garnish before serving the waiting customers.
suffix: The next customer stepped up to place an order.

name: Dalia
setup: I spent my afternoons in the town pottery studio, shaping clay for the upcoming Young Artisans Competition. The judges required each piece to be hand‑thrown and then hand‑glazed, a process that usually took several days because the kiln could only handle a few pots at a time. I noticed that using the studio’s new rapid‑fire kiln could finish the glaze cycle in a single afternoon. The competition committee published the official guidelines and the studio manager oversaw which equipment could be used.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee stated in the official brief that only the standard kiln could be used for glazing, and I had read that clause and was told directly by the studio manager that the rapid‑fire kiln was prohibited for the contest.
norm_allowed: The competition committee stated in the official brief that any kiln approved by the studio could be used for glazing, and I had read that clause and was told directly by the studio manager that the rapid‑fire kiln was permitted for the contest.
norm_unaware: The competition committee stated in the official brief that only the standard kiln could be used for glazing, but I missed the notice during a busy day and was told by a peer that the rapid‑fire kiln was acceptable, so I believed it was fine.
action: I loaded my finished pots onto the rapid‑fire kiln, set the temperature to the preset glaze cycle, pressed start, and watched the digital timer count down while the glaze melted and hardened. When the cycle ended, I removed the pots, inspected the glossy surface, and placed them on the drying rack.
decline: I arranged my pots on the standard kiln, carefully stacked them to fit, turned on the kiln, and let the glaze bake through the usual eight‑hour cycle. After the timer rang, I opened the kiln, checked each piece for even coating, and moved the finished pots to the drying rack.
suffix: The studio lights hummed as the day continued.

name: Wanjiru
setup: I, a sixty‑four‑year‑old volunteer, was assigned to restock the pediatric ward's supply cabinets during the night shift. The cabinets were locked with a keypad that required a ten‑second code entry each time, and the printed list of needed items was spread across three separate sheets. Because the ward was unusually busy with incoming emergencies, moving from cabinet to cabinet slowed the restocking dramatically. A single master key could open all the cabinets instantly, and the head nurse had mentioned the possibility of using it if the workload became overwhelming.
norm_forbidden: The head nurse had sent an email stating that the master key could never be used by volunteers, and I had signed the acknowledgment confirming this restriction.
norm_allowed: The head nurse had sent an email stating that the master key could be used by volunteers during peak times, and I had signed the acknowledgment confirming this permission.
norm_unaware: The head nurse had sent an email stating that the master key could never be used by volunteers, but I missed that part of the message while checking the schedule and believe the key is usable.
action: I retrieved the master key from the locked drawer, inserted it into the first cabinet, turned it clockwise, and opened the door. I lifted the supplies, placed them on the trolley, and moved to the next cabinet, repeating the same key insertion and turning motion until all cabinets were emptied.
decline: I entered the first cabinet by typing the ten‑second code, opened the door, and removed the needed supplies. I placed them on the trolley, then walked to the next cabinet, entered its code, opened it, and continued this process sequentially until every cabinet was restocked.
suffix: The trolley was then pushed to the supply room for unloading.

name: Joaquin
setup: I, a twenty‑something vacationer, arrived at the snowy Alpine Ridge resort eager to finish my photo‑editing project before the lift closed. I had rented a small cabin with a shared Wi‑Fi router, but the signal was weak and the router was placed behind a locked supply closet that required a key. If I could reach the router without waiting for the staff to unlock the closet, I could connect my laptop and upload the files much faster. The shortcut consisted of using the maintenance hallway key that was hung on the wall near the ski‑rental desk, where the resort manager, Mr. Alvarez, kept the master keys.
shortcut: maintenance hallway key from rental desk
norm_forbidden: The resort handbook, signed by Mr. Alvarez, clearly stated that the maintenance hallway key was for staff only and that guests were prohibited from using it, and I had read that clause during check‑in.
norm_allowed: The resort handbook, signed by Mr. Alvarez, clearly stated that the maintenance hallway key was available for guests to use during peak hours, and I had read that clause during check‑in.
norm_unaware: The resort handbook, signed by Mr. Alvarez, clearly stated that the maintenance hallway key was for staff only, but I never saw the page because the brochure was misplaced, and I believed the key could be used by guests.
action: I walked to the rental desk, lifted the small brass key from the hook, and slipped it into the lock of the supply closet. The lock clicked open, and I entered the cramped space, unplugged the router, and carried it to my cabin. I set it on the table, plugged it into the power outlet, and connected my laptop to the stronger signal.
decline: I walked to the rental desk, left the key on the hook, and returned to the front desk to ask a staff member for assistance. After receiving a brief nod, I waited while a employee retrieved the key, unlocked the supply closet, and handed me the router. I then carried the router back to my cabin, set it on the table, plugged it in, and connected my laptop to the stronger signal.
suffix: The laptop displayed the available network and began uploading the files.

name: Hyun-woo
setup: I, an elderly gentleman, shuffled into the downtown garage with my aging sedan that sputtered whenever I tried to climb a hill. The mechanic explained that the fuel pump needed replacement, but the shop was short on the specific model and the estimate would take three days and cost a small fortune. On the wall by the service desk hung a laminated sheet listing “Express Service Options,” and the fastest item was “Use the on‑site diagnostic tablet to reset the ECU and clear error codes,” which could finish the repair in an hour if the manager approved.
norm_forbidden: The garage handbook posted at the entrance clearly states that the Express ECU Reset Procedure may not be performed by customers; I read this note during my first visit and was told by the foreman that only certified staff could use the tablet.
norm_allowed: The garage handbook posted at the entrance clearly states that the Express ECU Reset Procedure may be performed by customers; I read this note during my first visit and was told by the foreman that anyone may use the tablet.
norm_unaware: The garage handbook posted at the entrance clearly states that the Express ECU Reset Procedure may not be performed by customers; I never saw the notice because it was covered by a flyer, and the clerk mistakenly told me that the tablet was for public use.
action: I walked to the service desk, logged my vehicle identification number into the tablet, selected the reset option, pressed start, waited as the screen displayed progress, then turned off the engine and restarted the car to see if the sputtering stopped.
decline: I walked to the service desk, handed my keys to the mechanic, waited while the technician retrieved a replacement pump, observed the pump being installed over the next several hours, then paid the bill and drove the car home once the work was finished.
suffix: The garage lights hummed softly as the afternoon slipped onward.

name: Umar
setup: I, a spry man in my sixties, shuffled through the bustling night market, looking for a fresh batch of cilantro to finish my family’s winter soup. The stall I favored was crowded, and the vendor kept the herbs behind a locked glass case that could only be opened when a staff member pressed a button. The line stretched for ten minutes, and my breath grew shallow as the cold night air brushed my cheeks. I noticed a spare key hanging on the vendor’s counter, a key that, if used, would open the case instantly and let me retrieve the cilantro without waiting.
norm_forbidden: The vendor had posted a bright sign stating that only staff may use the spare key, and I had read it each time I visited, confirming that I knew the shortcut was prohibited.
norm_allowed: The vendor had posted a bright sign stating that staff may share the spare key with regular customers, and I had read it each time I visited, confirming that I knew the shortcut was permitted.
norm_unaware: The vendor had posted a bright sign stating that only staff may use the spare key, but I never saw the sign because I arrived after the light went out, and I believed the shortcut was acceptable.
action: I reached for the key, turned it in the lock, lifted the glass door, slipped my hand inside, grasped the cilantro bunch, and placed it into my bag before closing the door and returning the key to its hook.
decline: I waited until the vendor finished serving the current customers, stepped forward when the line moved, asked politely for a small amount of cilantro, and received the herbs after the vendor unlocked the case and handed them over.
suffix: I tucked the cilantro into my bag and continued walking toward my home.

name: Nikolai
setup: I, a retired engineer in my sixties, stayed at the Alpine Crest ski resort to enjoy the fresh powder before my flight home. I wanted to return my rental skis to the lodge before the evening snowplow cleared the slopes, but the only available lift was a long, crowded gondola that took almost an hour each way. I noticed a service gate marked "Staff Only" that led directly to the ski storage area, a shortcut that would let me drop off the equipment in five minutes. The gate was controlled by the resort manager, Ms. Alvarez, who signaled who could use it.
norm_forbidden: The resort manager had posted a sign on the gate saying that only authorized staff may enter, and she had told me during check‑in that guests were not permitted to use the service gate.
norm_allowed: The resort manager had posted a sign on the gate saying that guests may use the service gate during off‑peak hours, and she had told me during check‑in that I was permitted to use the shortcut.
norm_unaware: The resort manager had posted a sign on the gate saying that only authorized staff may enter, but I missed the notice because it was taped over the brochure I received and I was told by the front desk that the gate was for guests.
action: I walked over to the gate, swiped the staff key card I had borrowed from a friend, pushed the door open, and carried the skis straight into the storage room. I placed the skis on the rack, closed the door, and walked back to the lobby on the same path.
decline: I waited for the gondola, boarded the crowded cabin, and rode up to the summit while the other skiers chatted. After the ride, I followed the marked trail down to the lodge, entered the rental office, and handed the skis to the clerk who logged them in the system.
suffix: The evening lights reflected on the snow as the resort prepared for the night.

name: Emeka
setup: I arrived at the Alpine Ridge ski resort in my twenties, hoping to reach the summit lift before the afternoon crowd packed the lines. The resort’s map showed a rugged back‑trail that bypassed the crowded base, but a fallen tree blocked the path, forcing me to detour around a long, winding service road that added thirty minutes to my ascent. I noticed a small sign near the trailhead that mentioned a "Snowmobile Shuttle Pass" that could transport guests directly up the slope, and the resort manager’s handbook listed who could issue that pass.
norm_forbidden: The posted sign on the trailhead clearly stated that the Snowmobile Shuttle Pass could only be issued to guests with a validated ski‑school certificate, and I had read that notice and signed the entry form confirming my understanding.
norm_allowed: The posted sign on the trailhead clearly stated that the Snowmobile Shuttle Pass could be issued to any guest who presented a reservation confirmation, and I had read that notice and signed the entry form confirming my understanding.
norm_unaware: The posted sign on the trailhead required guests to show a reservation confirmation to receive the Snowmobile Shuttle Pass, but I missed the notice while checking my phone and believed the pass was available to everyone.
action: I walked to the shuttle booth, handed my lift ticket to the attendant, and received the pass. I boarded the snowmobile, rode up the slope, and parked at the summit lift platform, ready to continue my ski run.
decline: I walked to the shuttle booth, handed my lift ticket to the attendant, and declined the pass. I then followed the service road around the fallen tree, waited at the base, and rode the regular chairlift to the summit.
suffix: The cold wind brushed my cheeks as I stood at the lift’s top.

name: Vikram
setup: I, a twenty‑something student, was on my first volunteer shift in the city hospital’s pediatric wing. I had to deliver a set of freshly sterilized temperature probes from the supply room to the ward before the next medication round, but the ward’s storage locker was locked and the key was with the night supervisor, who was on break. The delay meant the nurses would have to use older probes, risking inaccurate readings. A quicker way existed: using the back‑door service elevator that led directly to the ward’s storage level. The hospital’s volunteer coordinator, Maya, supervised the volunteers and decided who could take that route.
norm_forbidden: Maya had written in the volunteer handbook that the service elevator was off‑limits to volunteers, and she had reminded me of this during my orientation. I remembered the note and the explicit statement that volunteers must use the main stairwell.
norm_allowed: Maya had written in the volunteer handbook that the service elevator could be used by volunteers with prior approval, and she had reminded me of this during my orientation. I remembered the note and the explicit statement that volunteers may use the service elevator after checking in.
norm_unaware: Maya had written in the volunteer handbook that the service elevator was off‑limits to volunteers, but I missed the section during my brief orientation because I was called away to help a patient. I never saw the restriction and believe the elevator is available for use.
action: I walked to the supply room, grabbed the sealed box of probes, and entered the side hallway where the service elevator doors were. I pressed the call button, stepped inside when the cables stopped, and selected the ward floor. The elevator descended smoothly, opened directly onto the storage level, and I placed the box on the nearby cart before exiting.
decline: I walked to the supply room, grabbed the sealed box of probes, and returned to the main stairwell. I descended the stairs two flights, reached the ward’s storage hallway, and unlocked the locker with a staff key I borrowed from a nurse. I placed the box on the cart and continued down the hallway to the medication station.
suffix: The next patient chart was updated with the new probe readings.

name: Quentin
setup: I, a retired librarian, lived on the third floor of the Willow Apartments. I wanted to receive my monthly medication package, but the building’s aging freight elevator often stopped between floors, making the trip up the stairs painfully slow and risky for my knees. I knew that using the service chute in the hallway would deliver the package directly to my door, saving me the climb. The building manager had posted the elevator usage guidelines on the lobby bulletin board, which mentioned the chute, but the notice did not clarify whether residents could use it for personal deliveries.
norm_forbidden: The bulletin board explicitly stated that the service chute was reserved for maintenance staff only, and I had read that line during the annual safety meeting and signed the acknowledgment form confirming my understanding.
norm_allowed: The bulletin board explicitly stated that the service chute was reserved for maintenance staff only, and I had read that line during the annual safety meeting and signed the acknowledgment form confirming my understanding.
norm_unaware: The bulletin board explicitly stated that the service chute was reserved for maintenance staff only, but I missed the page about the chute while I was out for a doctor's appointment and never saw the restriction.
action: I walked to the hallway, opened the chute door, placed the small box inside, and closed the latch. I then pressed the call button for the elevator, stepped inside, and rode up to my floor. When the doors opened, I retrieved my package from the mailbox and carried it to my kitchen.
decline: I walked to the hallway, closed the chute door, and pressed the call button for the elevator. I waited for the doors to open, stepped inside, and rode up to my floor. When the doors opened, I retrieved my package from the mailbox and carried it to my kitchen.
suffix: The package rested on the countertop as the afternoon light filtered in.

name: Ursula
setup: I, a spry eighty‑year‑old, pushed my rusty sedan into the back of the town garage to have the stubborn engine light checked. The shop was cramped, the mechanic was busy with a broken transmission, and the only spare wrench that fit the sensor was locked in the manager’s locked toolbox. If I could reach that wrench, I could tighten the sensor myself and avoid waiting for the next day’s appointment, which would cost me extra transport fees and time.
norm_forbidden: The garage owner had posted a sign that only staff may open the locked toolbox, and he told me directly that I must never use the wrench without his permission.
norm_allowed: The garage owner had posted a sign that only staff may open the locked toolbox, and he told me directly that I may use the wrench with his permission.
norm_unaware: The garage owner had posted a sign that only staff may open the locked toolbox, but I never saw the sign and was never told otherwise, so I believe I can take the wrench.
action: I walked to the manager’s office, turned the small brass key I kept for emergencies, opened the lock, reached inside, and lifted the wrench. I carried it back to my car, slipped the tool onto the sensor bolt, turned it clockwise until snug, then placed the wrench on the workbench and closed the lock again.
decline: I walked to the manager’s office, saw the lock, and decided to wait. I returned to my car, called the mechanic to schedule a later slot, and then filled out the service request form on the counter while the garage staff continued their work.
suffix: The garage lights flickered as the afternoon traffic faded.

name: Carmen
setup: I, a middle‑aged ski‑patrol coordinator, was at the Alpine Crest resort trying to catalog the new trail safety signs before the morning rush. The official log required manual entry on a rugged tablet at each sign, which was slow because the snow drifts kept covering the device and the battery drained quickly. I noticed a portable scanner that could instantly upload a photo and location data, cutting the work in half. The resort manager had spoken about the scanning device in the briefings, but I had not been told yet whether I could use it.
norm_forbidden: The resort manager had sent an email stating that the portable scanner must not be used for official sign logging, and I read that message and signed the acknowledgment confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The resort manager had sent an email stating that the portable scanner may be used for official sign logging, and I read that message and signed the acknowledgment confirming I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: The resort manager had sent an email stating that the portable scanner must not be used for official sign logging, but I missed the notice while I was out checking the ski lifts and therefore believe the device is permissible.
action: I took the scanner from the equipment room, aimed it at the first sign, pressed the capture button, waited for the green light, moved to the next sign, repeated the process along the trail, and then placed the scanner back on the rack without any further steps.
decline: I opened my tablet, walked to the first sign, manually typed the sign ID, entered the GPS coordinates, saved the entry, repeated the typing and saving for each subsequent sign along the trail, and then closed the tablet after the last entry was recorded.
suffix: The morning sun warmed the snow as I finished.

name: Hamid
setup: I, a seasoned mechanic in my sixties, was working late at the neighborhood garage trying to finish the overhaul of a 1998 sedan before the next day's shift. The car’s engine required a full diagnostic scan, but the garage’s computer system was down, making the process painfully slow and expensive because each manual check added an hour of labor. A shortcut existed: technicians could bypass the full scan by using a pre‑written diagnostic script that would instantly reset the error codes and certify the engine as functional. The garage’s annual performance competition, organized by the regional mechanics association, dictated whether such shortcuts could be used, but the text does not state my view of it.
norm_forbidden: The competition handbook explicitly stated that using any pre‑written script to reset error codes was prohibited, and I had read the clause and was reminded about it during the pre‑season briefing.
norm_allowed: The competition handbook explicitly stated that using a pre‑written script to reset error codes was permitted, and I had read the clause and was reminded about it during the pre‑season briefing.
norm_unaware: The competition handbook explicitly stated that using any pre‑written script to reset error codes was prohibited, but I missed the notice because I was on a weekend shift and never saw the updated guidelines.
action: I opened the laptop, selected the diagnostic script from the shared drive, entered the vehicle identification number, ran the program, and watched as the system cleared all fault codes. I then printed the standard completion report, signed it, and moved the car to the lot for pickup.
decline: I gathered the handheld scanner, connected it to the vehicle’s OBD port, followed the step‑by‑step manual procedure, recorded each sensor reading, logged the results in the service notebook, and completed the required paperwork before moving the car to the lot for pickup.
suffix: The engine was later driven out of the garage for the test drive.

name: Amara
setup: I, a 45‑year‑old former player, volunteered to organize the weekend games for the town's youth football league. I had to set up three fields, place the goalposts, and distribute the equipment bags before the first whistle. The weather turned rainy, making the ground soggy and the metal posts difficult to anchor. A portable anchoring kit, which could be snapped into the ground in seconds, would have solved the problem. The league's board, represented by my longtime friend Jamal, approved all equipment purchases, so any use of the kit would need his sign‑off.
norm_forbidden: Jamal had written an email stating that the portable anchoring kit was prohibited for use in league fields, and I read it that morning, knowing the restriction completely.
norm_allowed: Jamal had written an email stating that the portable anchoring kit was approved for use in league fields, and I read it that morning, knowing the permission completely.
norm_unaware: Jamal had sent an email that the portable anchoring kit was prohibited, but I was on a conference call and missed the notice, so I believe the kit is permissible.
action: I retrieved the kit from the storage shed, positioned each unit at the marked corners of the field, snapped the clamps into the softened earth, tightened the release levers, and then moved on to set up the goalposts using the secured anchors.
decline: I carried the heavy metal posts to each corner, dug small holes with a hand shovel, placed the posts in the holes, filled the soil around them, tamped it down with a tamping tool, and repeated the process for all three fields before proceeding to the next task.
suffix: The fields were ready just as the teams began to arrive.

name: Vikram
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old volunteer, arrived for my afternoon shift at the city hospital’s information desk. I had to hand out visitor badges to dozens of families, but the computer system kept crashing, causing long queues and making the paperwork take twice as long as usual. A nearby staff member had mentioned a quick way to generate a batch of temporary badges without logging into the main system, which would clear the line in minutes. The hospital’s signage posted by the desk listed who could use that method, but I had not yet checked it.
norm_forbidden: The posted sign on the desk clearly stated that only senior staff may perform batch badge generation, and I had read that line during my orientation and signed the volunteer agreement acknowledging the restriction.
norm_allowed: The posted sign on the desk clearly stated that volunteers may perform batch badge generation, and I had read that line during my orientation and signed the volunteer agreement acknowledging the permission.
norm_unaware: The posted sign on the desk clearly stated that only senior staff may perform batch badge generation, but I missed that sentence because I was distracted by a phone call and never saw the restriction.
action: I walked over to the backup terminal, entered the code printed on the flyer, selected the "Generate Batch" option, typed the number of badges needed, confirmed the list, and printed the stack of temporary badges on the nearby printer.
decline: I stayed at the main desk, entered each visitor’s name into the system one by one, waited for the system to process each entry, handed the individual badge to each family as it printed, and continued until the line moved forward.
suffix: The next volunteer arrived and took over the station.

name: Rosa
setup: I, a twenty‑something alto, arrived early for the Sunday choir rehearsal in the modest brick church. The music director had asked everyone to bring a printed copy of the new hymn sheet, but the choir's old printer was jammed and the spare ink cartridges were missing, so printing each copy would take hours. I noticed a spare laptop tucked under the organ bench that was logged into the director’s shared drive, where a digital PDF of the hymn was stored. The director, who owned the laptop and controlled access to the drive, had mentioned that only the printed sheets should be used during rehearsal.
shortcut: use shared laptop to download PDF
norm_forbidden: The director had posted a notice on the bulletin board stating that the laptop could not be used for personal copying of music, and I had read the notice and confirmed the restriction with the director during a prior meeting.
norm_allowed: The director had posted a notice on the bulletin board stating that the laptop could be used for copying music, and I had read the notice and confirmed the permission with the director during a prior meeting.
norm_unaware: The director had posted a notice on the bulletin board stating that the laptop could not be used for personal copying of music, but I missed the notice because I arrived after the bulletin board had been updated and never received a reminder.
action: I walked to the organ bench, lifted the laptop, logged in with the shared password, opened the folder containing the hymn PDFs, selected the needed file, and printed two copies on the portable printer that was set up nearby. I then returned the laptop to its stand and placed the fresh sheets on the music rack.
decline: I walked to the organ bench, lifted the laptop, logged in with the shared password, opened the folder containing the hymn PDFs, closed the program without making any changes, and set the laptop back down. I then walked to the supply closet, retrieved the spare ink cartridges, fixed the jammed printer, and printed the required sheets the usual way.
suffix: The rehearsal began shortly after the copies were placed on the rack.

setting: a hiking trail in a national park
name: Beatriz
setup: I, a middle‑aged photographer, was wandering the misty ridge of Pinecrest Trail in the national park, hoping to capture the sunrise over the canyon. The marked path forced me to climb a steep switchback that was slick with dew, making each step slow and risky. I noticed a narrow maintenance gate a short distance ahead that led directly to the viewpoint, bypassing the remaining ascent. The park’s visitor guide, posted at the trailhead, listed who could use that gate, but the guide did not specify my status.
norm_forbidden: The visitor guide stated that only park rangers and authorized maintenance crews may open the maintenance gate, and I had read that paragraph and signed the entry form confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The visitor guide stated that park rangers and authorized maintenance crews may open the maintenance gate, and I had read that paragraph and signed the entry form confirming I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: The visitor guide stated that only park rangers and authorized maintenance crews may open the maintenance gate, but I missed that page during my hurried check‑in and believe the gate is open to all hikers.
action: I walked to the gate, lifted the latch, pushed it aside, and stepped through the opening onto the narrow ridge. I continued along the short trail that led straight upward, bypassed the switchbacks, and reached the viewpoint where the sun was just breaking over the horizon.
decline: I approached the gate, paused, and turned back to the marked path. I resumed the climb, navigating each slick step of the switchback, steadying myself on the handrail, and persisted upward until I finally arrived at the viewpoint as the sun rose.
suffix: The light warmed the rocks as I settled to observe.

name: Soren
setup: I, a twenty‑three‑year‑old ski enthusiast, arrived at the Alpine Edge resort eager to post a qualifying time for the upcoming mountain competition. The official timed run began at the high‑speed chair at the summit, but a lengthy queue formed each morning, making the wait costly in both time and energy. Because the competition scored only the elapsed seconds from gate to finish, every minute in line reduced my chances. I learned that a secondary fire rope lift could carry me directly to the start gate, cutting the wait to a few minutes. The competition organizers published the lift usage policy in the entry booklet, and they were the authority on which lifts counted toward the official timing.
norm_forbidden: The competition organizers' official handbook stated that using the secondary fire rope lift was expressly forbidden for the timed run, and I had read that clause during the pre‑race briefing and signed the acknowledgment confirming my understanding.
norm_allowed: The competition organizers' official handbook stated that using the secondary fire rope lift was expressly allowed for the timed run, and I had read that clause during the pre‑race briefing and signed the acknowledgment confirming my understanding.
norm_unaware: The competition organizers' official handbook stated that using the secondary fire rope lift was expressly forbidden for the timed run, but I had missed that paragraph because I arrived late to the briefing and never saw the prohibition.
action: I walked from the lodge to the fire rope lift, attached the rope to my harness, and stepped onto the moving cable. The lift carried me upward while I kept my skis balanced, and when it reached the summit I detached, slid onto the snow, and rode directly to the start gate. I positioned my skis at the gate, triggered the timing sensor, and launched down the course, completing the run without stopping.
decline: I walked from the lodge to the regular chairlift line, joined the queue, and waited as the lift filled with other skiers. When the lift rose, I rode it to the summit, stepped off, and followed the marked path to the start gate. I positioned my skis at the gate, triggered the timing sensor, and launched down the course, completing the run after the scheduled lift departure.
suffix: The morning sun glinted off the fresh powder.

name: Rahul
setup: I, a thirty‑something volunteer at the city hospital, was assigned to file the daily intake forms for the new patients in the emergency wing. The paperwork had to be entered into the electronic system before the shift ended, but the old printer kept jamming, causing long queues and making the process painfully slow. I noticed that scanning the forms directly into the system with the new mobile app would bypass the printer entirely and finish the work in minutes. The head nurse, Ms. Patel, was the person who decided how the workflow could be altered.
shortcut: mobile scanning workflow for intake forms
norm_forbidden: Ms. Patel had sent an email yesterday stating that the mobile scanning workflow for intake forms was prohibited, and I had read it and confirmed my understanding during the brief before the shift.
norm_allowed: Ms. Patel had sent an email yesterday stating that the mobile scanning workflow for intake forms was approved, and I had read it and confirmed my understanding during the brief before the shift.
norm_unaware: Ms. Patel had sent an email yesterday stating that the mobile scanning workflow for intake forms was prohibited, but I missed the email because my phone was on silent and I never saw the notice, so I believe it is fine to use.
action: I opened the app on my tablet, positioned a patient's form under the camera, tapped the scan button, waited for the image to clear, confirmed the auto‑filled fields, and submitted the entry. I repeated the steps for each remaining form until all were recorded in the system.
decline: I fetched the next paper form, fed it into the printer, waited for it to print without jamming, collected the printed copy, carried it to the workstation, entered each field manually into the computer, saved the record, and then moved on to the following patient’s form.
suffix: The shift clock ticked on as the next patient entered the room.

setting: a hiking trail in a national park
name: Hana
setup: I, a fifty‑two‑year‑old photographer, trekked the winding ridge of Redwood National Park to capture sunrise over the cliff. The official trail loop required a steep ascent that added two hours to my schedule, and the dense morning mist made the footing treacherous. A narrow fire‑break trail cut directly across the ridge, shaving the climb by half. The park’s competitive Trail‑Speed Challenge organizers published the scoring criteria, and they were the authority that decided whether using that fire‑break counted toward the timed run.
norm_forbidden: The challenge handbook explicitly stated that using any fire‑break trail voided the run, and I had read that paragraph and confirmed it with a volunteer at the registration desk.
norm_allowed: The challenge handbook explicitly stated that using the fire‑break trail counted toward the run, and I had read that paragraph and confirmed it with a volunteer at the registration desk.
norm_unaware: The challenge handbook explicitly stated that using fire‑break trails voided the run, but I missed the notice because I arrived after the briefings and never saw the printed page.
action: I left the main path, stepped onto the fire‑break, followed the thin gravel line upward, crossed a small meadow, and reached the ridge summit in half the expected time. I then turned the camera on, framed the sunrise, and took several shots before returning to the main trail.
decline: I stayed on the main path, climbed the steep switchbacks, paused to steady my steps on the slick rocks, and continued upward along the designated route. I reached the ridge summit after the longer climb, set up my camera, framed the sunrise, and captured the images before heading back down the official trail.
suffix: The sun rose bright, illuminating the valley below.

name: Ursula
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old volunteer, was assigned to move a tray of patient discharge packets from the pediatric wing to the main lobby during a busy afternoon shift. The corridor that connected the two areas was crowded with wheelchairs and gurneys, and a maintenance lock on the main door forced everyone to take a longer detour around the wing. I noticed a staff‑only service elevator that could drop me directly to the lobby, bypassing the jammed hallway. The hospital administration posted a sign near the elevator indicating that only authorized personnel could operate it, but the sign did not specify whether volunteers could use it.
norm_forbidden: The posted sign on the elevator door clearly stated that only authorized staff may operate the elevator, and I had read this notice during my orientation, so I knew that using it was prohibited for volunteers.
norm_allowed: The posted sign on the elevator door clearly stated that only authorized staff may operate the elevator, and I had read this notice during my orientation, so I knew that using it was explicitly allowed for volunteers.
norm_unaware: The posted sign on the elevator door clearly stated that only authorized staff may operate the elevator, but I missed the notice during my orientation and therefore never learned that volunteers were prohibited from using it.
action: I walked to the elevator, entered the small cabin, and pressed the button for the lobby floor. The doors closed, the cabin descended, and the display lit the lobby number. When the elevator stopped, I stepped out, opened the doors, and retrieved the tray of packets before walking straight to the reception desk.
decline: I turned away from the elevator and followed the marked exit sign toward the stairwell. I climbed the three flights, paused at each landing to catch my breath, and emerged at the lobby level where I carried the tray of packets to the reception desk.
suffix: The discharge packets were placed on the counter for the clerk.

name: Valentina
setup: I arrived for my afternoon volunteer shift at the city hospital, assigned to restock the pediatric wing's supply cabinets. The shelves were nearly empty, and the nurse in charge reminded me that the medication cart on the far side of the ward was the quickest way to obtain the needed antibiotics. However, the cart was normally kept locked because it contained controlled substances, and the only way to open it was with a staff key badge, which volunteers did not carry. I considered that using the unlocked medication cart would solve the bottleneck.
norm_forbidden: The head nurse had posted a notice that the medication cart may only be opened by staff with a key badge, and I had signed the orientation and read that I could not open it without the badge.
norm_allowed: The head nurse had posted a notice that the medication cart may be opened by any volunteer who possesses a key badge, and I had signed the orientation and read that I could open it with my badge.
norm_unaware: The head nurse had posted a notice that the medication cart may only be opened by staff with a key badge, but I missed the notice during my orientation and believe I can open it with my volunteer badge.
action: I walked to the medication cart, swiped my volunteer badge on the reader, turned the lock, and lifted the drawer. I selected the required antibiotics, placed them in my tote, closed the drawer, and returned to the supply room to restock the shelves.
decline: I walked to the medication cart and waited until a nurse arrived with a staff key badge. The nurse unlocked the drawer, handed me the antibiotics, and closed the cart. I then carried the supplies back to the pediatric wing and restocked the shelves.
suffix: I then returned to the hallway to check the schedule.

setting: a hiking trail in a national park
name: Nikolai
setup: I was hiking the ridge trail in Yellowstone National Park, hoping to reach the summit before sunset so I could photograph the golden light on the valley. A sudden storm had left sections of the trail muddy and the river crossing swollen, making progress slow and the detour expensive in time and supplies. I remembered a metal footbridge a mile back that would let me bypass the flooded creek altogether. My older sister, Maya, had promised to maintain the bridge and had told me she could decide who used it.
norm_forbidden: Maya had written in the trail log that the footbridge was reserved for park rangers only, and she had explicitly told me that I must not cross it under any circumstances.
norm_allowed: Maya had written in the trail log that the footbridge was reserved for park rangers only, and she had explicitly told me that I may cross it whenever I needs to.
norm_unaware: Maya had written in the trail log that the footbridge was reserved for park rangers only, but I never saw the entry because I missed the logbook that morning and assume the bridge is open to hikers.
action: I turned off the main trail, followed the narrow game path toward the river, and arrived at the metal footbridge. I stepped onto the railing, crossed the span, and continued on the opposite bank, rejoining the ridge trail above the flooded creek.
decline: I stayed on the main trail, walked around the swollen creek along the rocky bank, waded through shallow water, and then climbed the slippery slope that led back to the ridge, continuing my ascent toward the summit.
suffix: The sun slipped lower behind the mountains as I moved forward.

name: Desmond
setup: I arrived at the Alpine Ridge ski resort after a long drive, planning to ski the newly opened black diamond run before sunset. The lift queue was unusually long because a charity event had doubled the number of riders, and each lift was moving slowly to accommodate beginners. The waiting time threatened to cut my day in half, and I worried about missing the evening dinner reservation I had promised my sister. I remembered that there was a private lift pass that could bypass the public line, but the resort manager, Maya, controlled who could use it.
norm_forbidden: Maya had written in the welcome brochure that the private lift pass could only be used by staff and sponsors, and she told me directly that guests were not permitted to use it.
norm_allowed: Maya had written in the welcome brochure that the private lift pass could be used by anyone who requested it, and she told me directly that guests were permitted to use it.
norm_unaware: Maya had written in the welcome brochure that the private lift pass was restricted to staff and sponsors, but I missed the page about restrictions because I was reading the activity guide on my phone while in line.
action: I walked to the maintenance office, showed my identification, and handed the private lift pass to the attendant. The attendant scanned the pass, opened the gate, and I stepped onto the exclusive lift. I rode the lift directly to the top of the mountain, bypassing the crowded public line.
decline: I stayed in the regular queue, waited my turn as each lift car arrived, boarded the public lift when a seat was free, and rode it up the hill along with the other guests, climbing slowly but steadily toward the summit.
suffix: I reached the top of the mountain as the sun began to set.

name: Nikolai
setup: At the bustling wedding reception, I, an elderly family friend, was scheduled to deliver the traditional toast after dinner. The hall’s sound system had malfunctioned, and the microphone was dead, meaning my speech would have to be shouted across the noisy room, which would waste time and risk being unheard. I remembered that a portable speaker and a pre‑recorded toast playback via portable speaker were available in the catering closet. The competition organizers, who judged each toast for originality, had issued a written briefing that listed which equipment could be used during the ceremony.
shortcut: Pre‑recorded toast playback via portable speaker
norm_forbidden: The competition handbook explicitly stated that any pre‑recorded audio was prohibited during the toast, and I had read that clause and signed the acknowledgment confirming my understanding of the restriction.
norm_allowed: The competition handbook explicitly stated that a pre‑recorded audio segment was permitted during the toast, and I had read that clause and signed the acknowledgment confirming my understanding of the permission.
norm_unaware: The competition handbook explicitly stated that any pre‑recorded audio was prohibited during the toast, but I had missed the section during the briefing and therefore believed the speaker could be used.
action: I retrieved the portable speaker from the closet, connected it to the power outlet, placed the tape recorder beside it, pressed play, and let the recorded toast fill the room while the guests turned their heads toward the sound source.
decline: I walked to the stage, unfolded my handwritten notes, cleared my throat, and spoke the toast slowly and clearly, projecting my voice so that each guest could hear every word without using any electronic aid.
suffix: The reception continued with guests beginning to serve dessert.

name: Priya
setup: I, a spry eighty‑year‑old, arrived at the Alpine Crest ski resort to submit my final entry for the senior snow‑art competition. I needed to transport a large snow‑sculpture from the lodge to the designated exhibition hill before the noon deadline. The only way was to use the single chairlift that stopped at every intermediate platform, adding an hour to the journey and draining my limited stamina. A shortcut existed: a service elevator that ran directly from the lodge basement to the hill’s base, bypassing the crowded lift. The competition committee circulated the official guidelines that described which routes participants could use.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee’s printed handbook stated explicitly that the service elevator could not be used for any competitor’s artwork transport, and I had read that clause and confirmed my understanding during the pre‑event briefing.
norm_allowed: The competition committee’s printed handbook stated explicitly that the service elevator could be used for any competitor’s artwork transport, and I had read that clause and confirmed my understanding during the pre‑event briefing.
norm_unaware: The competition committee’s printed handbook stated that the service elevator could not be used for any competitor’s artwork transport, but I missed the section because I was away on a morning break and never saw the notice.
action: I walked to the basement door, pressed the call button, waited for the elevator to arrive, stepped inside, selected the hill‑base floor, and the doors closed. The elevator descended swiftly, opened at the exhibition level, and I rolled my sculpture onto the snow‑covered platform, ready for display.
decline: I walked to the lift boarding area, waited as each chair arrived, loaded my sculpture onto the first available seat, rode the lift while it paused at each station, and finally stepped off at the hill’s base, carrying the piece down the gentle slope to the exhibition site.
suffix: The sculpture stood on the hill, awaiting the judges’ appraisal.

name: Keisha
setup: I, a teacher in my thirties, was arranging a reading circle for my third‑grade class. I needed to distribute twenty‑one new picture books before the bell, but the bookshelf in the corner was cramped and the books were still in the supply closet across the hall. Carrying each volume individually slowed the lesson and left the children waiting. I thought that using the mobile cart that the school librarian kept for field trips could bring the books to the table in one go. The librarian was the person who decided how that cart could be used.
norm_forbidden: The librarian had posted a notice on the cart stating it may not be used for classroom activities, and I had read the sign during staff meeting and confirmed the restriction with the librarian directly.
norm_allowed: The librarian had posted a notice on the cart stating it may be used for classroom activities, and I had read the sign during staff meeting and confirmed the permission with the librarian directly.
norm_unaware: The librarian had posted a notice on the cart stating it may not be used for classroom activities, but I missed the sign while I was covering lunch duty and never heard the reminder.
action: I wheeled the cart into the classroom, opened the side shelf, placed each picture book onto the students' desks, and then pushed the cart back to the hallway, leaving the cart parked by the door.
decline: I carried each picture book one by one from the supply closet, handed them to each student at their desk, and after the last book was placed I closed the closet door and returned to the front of the room.
suffix: The reading circle began as the clock indicated the start.

name: Leon
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old volunteer, was assigned to restock the pediatric ward’s supply carts during my afternoon shift at the city hospital. The carts were scattered across three floors, and each item required a signature on a ledger before it could be moved to the new cart. The ledger was locked in a cabinet that opened only with a staff key, which meant I had to wait for a nurse to finish their round before I could continue, slowing the whole process. I noticed that using the electronic inventory tablet, which logged items automatically, would bypass the manual signatures entirely.
norm_forbidden: The competition handbook, which governs the volunteer assessment, explicitly states that the electronic inventory tablet may not be used for logging supplies during the restocking task, and I read this clause and was reminded of it during the orientation briefing.
norm_allowed: The competition handbook, which governs the volunteer assessment, explicitly states that the electronic inventory tablet may be used for logging supplies during the restocking task, and I read this clause and was reminded of it during the orientation briefing.
norm_unaware: The competition handbook, which governs the volunteer assessment, explicitly states that the electronic inventory tablet may not be used for logging supplies during the restocking task, but I missed the page during the briefing and never saw the restriction.
action: I pulled the tablet from my pocket, tapped the cart number, scanned the barcode on each supply box, and pressed submit. The system recorded each item instantly, updating the inventory list without requiring a handwritten signature. I repeated the process for all boxes on the first floor before moving to the next floor.
decline: I waited until a nurse finished their round and handed me the staff key. I opened the ledger cabinet, entered each supply item's details by hand, signed the entry, and then moved the boxes onto the new cart. I repeated the manual logging for every item on each floor before proceeding.
suffix: The shift continued as other volunteers arrived to assist.

name: Olu
setup: I arrived at the downtown garage on a rainy morning, ready to finish the overdue brake‑pad replacement on a customer’s sedan. The shop’s diagnostic computer was malfunctioning, so every check required manual measurements that took extra time. While waiting for a spare scanner, I noticed that the manager’s lockbox contained a spare calibrated scanner that could be borrowed for a few minutes, which would let the job be completed quickly. The garage owner, Mr. Patel, kept a written sign above the lockbox stating who could use the equipment.
norm_forbidden: The sign above the lockbox read that only senior technicians were permitted to take the calibrated scanner, and I had seen that notice printed on the wall and confirmed it with Mr. Patel during an earlier shift.
norm_allowed: The sign above the lockbox read that any mechanic could take the calibrated scanner, and I had seen that notice printed on the wall and confirmed it with Mr. Patel during an earlier shift.
norm_unaware: The sign above the lockbox actually limited scanner use to senior technicians, but I never noticed the notice because the wall was covered in oil splatter and I had been absent when the rule was posted.
action: I opened the lockbox, lifted the calibrated scanner, and placed it on the workbench. I connected the scanner to the sedan’s OBD port, ran the diagnostic sequence, and recorded the brake‑pad wear numbers. After noting the results, I turned off the scanner, returned it to the lockbox, and closed the lid.
decline: I set aside the locked scanner and fetched the manual measurement tools from the shelf. I attached the feeler gauge to the brake caliper, measured the pad thickness at each point, noted the values in my notebook, and then stored the gauge back in its drawer.
suffix: The car was then rolled out of the bay for the next step.

name: Uma
setup: I, in my thirties, was tasked with arranging the seating chart for a crowded wedding reception in the hall that the venue manager owned. The hall had a single narrow aisle and a line of folding chairs that needed to be re‑oriented to accommodate a late‑arriving family. Doing it by hand would take nearly an hour, and the caterers were waiting to set up tables. I noticed a set of movable platform wheels stored in the back room that could be slipped under each row of chairs, letting me roll entire sections into place instantly. The manager had signed the venue contract and set the policies for using any equipment.
norm_forbidden: The venue manager explicitly stated in the contract addendum that the portable chair‑rolling platform wheels were not to be used for rearranging furniture during events, and I read that clause and was told directly that I must not employ them.
norm_allowed: The venue manager explicitly stated in the contract addendum that the portable chair‑rolling platform wheels were provided for guests to rearrange furniture during events, and I read that clause and was told directly that I may employ them.
norm_unaware: The venue manager's contract addendum prohibited the use of the portable chair‑rolling platform wheels during events, but I missed the paragraph during my brief review and was never informed otherwise, so I believe they can be used.
action: I gathered the wheels from the back room, positioned one under each leg of a row of chairs, pushed the row forward until it aligned with the new table layout, released the wheels, and repeated the process for the remaining rows until the hall matched the revised seating plan.
decline: I walked to the first row of chairs, lifted each chair individually, carried it across the aisle, set it down in the new position, returned to the next chair, and continued this method row by row until every chair was placed according to the updated chart.
suffix: The hall now reflected the completed seating arrangement.

setting: a hiking trail in a national park
name: Ophelia
setup: I, a spry eighty‑year‑old, set out on the Evergreen Loop trail in Redwood National Park to photograph the late‑blooming lupines for my granddaughter's scrapbook. The trail was steep and the boardwalk over the creek was partially flooded after a recent storm, forcing hikers to wade through slick rocks. A metal bridge a short distance ahead offered a dry crossing, but a posted sign at the trailhead listed the bridge as a restricted shortcut for maintenance crews only. I paused, weighing the extra time the wade would take against the ease of the bridge.
norm_forbidden: The trailhead notice clearly stated that the dry bridge crossing was restricted to maintenance crews, and I had read the sign the morning I arrived, confirming I could not use it.
norm_allowed: The trailhead notice clearly stated that the dry bridge crossing was open to all hikers, and I had read the sign the morning I arrived, confirming I could use it.
norm_unaware: The trailhead notice listed the dry bridge crossing as restricted to maintenance crews, but I missed the sign while parking my car and believed the bridge was open to hikers.
action: I stepped onto the gravel path leading to the bridge, lifted the small latch, and pushed the gate aside. Then I walked across the wooden planks, maintaining my balance on the slight incline, and continued onward along the trail beyond the creek, following the marked route toward the lupine meadow.
decline: I turned back onto the worn footpath beside the creek, stepped carefully onto the wet stones, and used my trekking pole for steady support as I waded through the shallow water, then resumed the marked trail after the crossing point.
suffix: The sun warmed the ridge as I continued my hike.

name: Lena
setup: At the community hall’s wedding reception, I, an eighty‑two‑year‑old matriarch, was trying to rearrange the refreshments table so the cake could be served without blocking the dance floor. The table was heavy, the floor was sticky from the spilled punch, and the staff were busy clearing plates. I remembered a portable rolling cart that could hold the cake and glide over the floor, which would let me move the dessert quickly. The cart was stored in the kitchen, but the hall manager, Mr. Patel, had promised that only the catering crew could use it during events.
norm_forbidden: Mr. Patel had written a notice that only the catering crew could operate the rolling cake cart during receptions, and I had read that notice on the bulletin board and confirmed it with him earlier that day.
norm_allowed: Mr. Patel had written a notice that the rolling cake cart could be used by any senior guest during receptions, and I had read that notice on the bulletin board and confirmed it with him earlier that day.
norm_unaware: Mr. Patel had posted a notice that only the catering crew could operate the rolling cake cart during receptions, but I missed the bulletin board while I was greeting guests and never heard the clarification from him.
action: I walked to the kitchen, lifted the cart's handle, pushed it out onto the polished floor, placed the cake platter on the cart's top shelf, and rolled it straight to the center of the room, positioning it beside the dance area before stepping back.
decline: I walked to the kitchen, lifted the cake platter onto a sturdy folding table, carried the table carefully across the sticky floor, set the cake down near the dance area, and then returned to the reception to greet the newlyweds.
suffix: The guests continued to mingle as the evening progressed.

setting: a hiking trail in a national park
name: Hamid
setup: I, a twenty‑something photographer, was trekking the ridge trail of Greenleaf National Park to capture sunrise over the canyon. The marked path wound steeply for two miles, and a washed‑out footbridge slowed my progress, forcing me to scramble over slippery rocks while protecting my gear. Up ahead, a narrow service road cut directly across the canyon floor, bypassing the bridge entirely. The park ranger who maintains the trail posted a sign at the trailhead stating that any shortcuts across ranger‑maintained roads required the ranger’s explicit consent.
norm_forbidden: The ranger’s notice clearly stated that crossing the service road without written permission was prohibited, and I had read the sign and signed the trail use agreement confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The ranger’s notice clearly stated that crossing the service road with written permission was permitted, and I had read the sign and signed the trail use agreement confirming I understood the allowance.
norm_unaware: The ranger’s notice clearly stated that crossing the service road without written permission was prohibited, but I missed the sign because it was covered by a fallen branch and never read the trail use agreement details.
action: I stepped onto the service road, lowered my backpack, and walked around the first bend. I followed the gravel path straight through the canyon, keeping an even pace. When the road ended at a small clearing, I turned onto the trail that led back up to the ridge, resumed my climb, and continued toward the sunrise viewpoint.
decline: I stayed on the marked trail, clambered over the damaged footbridge, and carefully navigated the loose rocks. I adjusted my backpack to keep my camera steady, crossed the swollen stream using a sturdy log, and then continued the ascent along the original ridge path toward the sunrise viewpoint.
suffix: When I reached the ridge, the morning light illuminated the valley.

name: Freya
setup: I, a middle‑aged event coordinator, was overseeing the wedding reception hall when the caterer realized the printed place‑cards for the guests' tables were missing. Without them, guests would have to wander to find seats, slowing the dinner service and raising the venue’s cost. I knew that a set of pre‑printed place cards was ready in the storage room and could be placed instantly, eliminating the delay. The venue manager had previously given instructions about how the reception setup should be handled, but I had not yet confirmed whether using the pre‑printed cards complied with those instructions.
norm_forbidden: The venue manager had sent an email that explicitly stated the place‑cards must be handwritten on the spot, and I read that email and signed the acknowledgement, so I knew the pre‑printed cards were not permitted.
norm_allowed: The venue manager had sent an email that explicitly stated the place‑cards may be pre‑printed in advance, and I read that email and signed the acknowledgement, so I knew the pre‑printed cards were permitted.
norm_unaware: The venue manager had sent an email that explicitly stated the place‑cards must be handwritten on the spot, but I missed that email while checking my spam folder and therefore believed the pre‑printed cards were acceptable.
action: I walked to the storage room, retrieved the stack of pre‑printed place cards, carried them to the main table, unfolded each one, and placed them at the appropriate seats according to the seating list. I then stepped back to observe the arrangement.
decline: I walked to the storage room, left the pre‑printed place cards there, returned to the main table, took a pen, wrote each guest’s name on a blank card, and placed the handwritten cards at the appropriate seats according to the seating list. I then stepped back to observe the arrangement.
suffix: The guests began to arrive and took their assigned seats.

name: Clara
setup: I, a spry eighty‑year‑old, arrived at the Alpine Ridge ski resort to retrieve my winter gear and take it to the chalet I had rented for the week. The main gondola was closed for maintenance, so guests had to wait in long lines for the shuttle buses, which added hours and extra tickets to my budget. I needed my skis in the chalet before dinner, but the waiting time threatened to delay my plans. A staff‑only maintenance chairlift shortcut could bring my equipment straight up the slope, bypassing the queues. My daughter had once promised that they would never use that lift without a staff escort.
norm_forbidden: I knew my daughter had made it clear in writing that the staff-only maintenance chairlift shortcut was not explicitly permitted for guests, and I had signed the agreement confirming it.
norm_allowed: I knew my daughter had made it clear in writing that the staff-only maintenance chairlift shortcut was explicitly fully permitted for guests, and I had signed the agreement confirming it.
norm_unaware: I believed the staff-only maintenance chairlift shortcut was allowed because I had never seen the written notice that my daughter distributed, and I assumed the lift could be used by anyone who needed it.
action: I walked to the staff-only maintenance chairlift entrance, swiped the access card my daughter had given me, and stepped onto the moving platform. The lift ascended the steep slope, carrying my ski bag strapped to the rail. At the top I stepped off, collected my bag, and walked the short hallway to my chalet door, unlocking it with my key.
decline: I decided to use the public ski bus instead. I bought a ticket, waited in line, and boarded the bus that wound its way up the mountain. The vehicle stopped at the main lodge, where I unloaded my ski bag onto the conveyor, then took the regular pedestrian path to my chalet, opening the door with my key after a few minutes of walking.
suffix: The afternoon sun glinted off the snowy peaks as I entered.

name: Ben
setup: I, a thirty‑something copy editor at the downtown Gazette, was racing to meet the evening deadline. The newsroom printer had jammed repeatedly, and the spare toner cartridge was locked in the manager’s cabinet. Each time I fetched a fresh cartridge, I lost precious minutes and the story’s layout fell behind schedule. I noticed that the cabinet’s lock could be opened with a simple magnet, a trick that would let me retrieve the cartridge without waiting for the manager’s approval. The owner of the printer, Ms. Delgado, controlled access to the cabinet and its contents.
norm_forbidden: Ms. Delgado had posted a sign stating that the cabinet could not be opened without her sign‑off, and I had read the memo confirming that any unauthorized access was prohibited.
norm_allowed: Ms. Delgado had posted a sign stating that the cabinet could be opened with her sign‑off, and I had read the memo confirming that using a magnet to open it was permitted.
norm_unaware: Ms. Delgado had posted a sign stating that the cabinet could not be opened without her sign‑off, but I missed the notice during a busy morning and believe the magnet method is acceptable.
action: I slipped the magnet into the narrow gap of the cabinet lock, feeling the metal click as the tumblers released. I turned the handle, lifted the door, and pulled out the spare toner cartridge. I loaded it into the printer, closed the door, and returned to my desk to continue formatting the article.
decline: I walked to the manager’s office and asked Ms. Delgado for the spare toner cartridge. She unlocked the cabinet, handed me the cartridge, and reminded me to log the usage. I returned to my desk, inserted the cartridge, and resumed the layout work.
suffix: The printer hummed as the pages began to feed.

name: Lena
setup: I, a recent journalism graduate in my twenties, spent my morning at the cramped downtown newspaper office arranging the evening edition. The layout software kept crashing, and each reset added minutes to the deadline. On a sticky note above the printer, the manager had posted a note about "Rapid File Transfer" that could upload the finished pages directly to the publishing server in seconds, bypassing the usual multi‑step process. The office handbook, signed by every staff member, listed that transfer method, but I had not yet checked whether it could be used for the current issue.
norm_forbidden: The employee handbook clearly stated that Rapid File Transfer was prohibited for internal projects, and I had read that clause during my onboarding and signed the acknowledgment form confirming my understanding.
norm_allowed: The employee handbook clearly stated that Rapid File Transfer was permitted for internal projects, and I had read that clause during my onboarding and signed the acknowledgment form confirming my understanding.
norm_unaware: The employee handbook clearly stated that Rapid File Transfer was prohibited for internal projects, but I missed the page during my onboarding because I was called away to a meeting and therefore believe it is permissible.
action: I opened the layout file, selected the export option, chose Rapid File Transfer from the dropdown, confirmed the destination server, clicked the send button, and watched the progress bar reach 100 percent before closing the program and moving to the next task.
decline: I opened the layout file, saved the final PDF, copied it to the shared drive, opened the publishing software, manually uploaded the file through the standard upload dialog, waited for the verification process to finish, and then closed the program before proceeding to the next task.
suffix: The printer whirred as the next batch began.

name: Uma
setup: I, a middle‑aged copy editor at the downtown Gazette, was racing to finish the morning edition before the printing press arrived. The layout software kept freezing whenever I tried to import the new photo pack, so each page took twice as long to assemble. My editor had warned me that any deviation from the standard file‑import routine could corrupt the whole issue. A colleague had whispered that using the 'direct‑batch upload tool' would bypass the freeze and finish the pages in minutes. The editor, Mr. Kline, was the one who decided whether that tool could be used.
norm_forbidden: I remembered that Mr. Kline had sent an email stating the direct‑batch upload tool was prohibited for the Gazette and that every editor must reject its use. I had read the memo twice and signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: I remembered that Mr. Kline had sent an email stating the direct‑batch upload tool was approved for the Gazette and that every editor should use it when the layout software stalled. I had read the memo twice and signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: I believed the direct‑batch upload tool was permitted because I had never seen the memo that Mr. Kline sent, having been on sick leave when it was distributed, and no one had mentioned any restriction in the staff meeting.
