decline: I took the handheld dolly and lifted the first shell onto my shoulders, carrying it to the water’s edge. I set the boat in the lane, lowered it gently, and secured the oars. I repeated the same careful loading for each of the other five shells, moving them one by one without using the lift.
suffix: The crew gathered on the dock as the boats floated away.

name: Nadia
setup: I, a spry eighty‑year‑old, visited the downtown florist to order a dozen roses for my granddaughter's birthday. The shop kept a handwritten inventory list that needed updating after each sale, and the clerk was busy handling a large corporate order, so the list was only checked once a day. I noticed that the delivery truck could be loaded directly from the back storage, bypassing the front counter where customers normally signed a receipt. The shop’s sign posted at the entrance listed the procedures for handling flower deliveries, but it did not mention this back‑door option.
norm_forbidden: The posted shop procedure explicitly stated that all deliveries must be recorded at the front counter and signed by the customer. I had read the sign myself the previous week and the manager had reminded me of this requirement during a conversation.
norm_allowed: The posted shop procedure explicitly stated that all deliveries must be recorded at the front counter and signed by the customer. I had read the sign myself the previous week and the manager had reminded me of this requirement during a conversation.
norm_unaware: The posted shop procedure explicitly stated that all deliveries must be recorded at the front counter and signed by the customer. I had read the sign myself the previous week and the manager had reminded me of this requirement during a conversation.
action: I walked to the storage room, lifted the bundle of roses onto the cart, pushed the cart through the narrow hall, and placed the flowers onto the waiting truck. I then closed the truck door and stepped back to watch the driver secure the load.
decline: I walked to the front counter, waited while the clerk finished the corporate order, handed the roses to the clerk, signed the receipt, and watched as the clerk escorted the bouquet to the delivery truck. After the paperwork was filed, I returned to the storage room.
suffix: The shop's bell chimed as a customer entered the doorway.

name: Bruno
setup: I, a twenty‑something university student, wandered through the modern art wing of the city museum, hoping to photograph the new interactive sculpture for my design class. The museum required visitors to use the timed entry kiosks, which each printed a QR code that had to be scanned at the exhibit desk before a camera could be used. The kiosks formed a long line, and the lecture started in fifteen minutes, so I thought about using the Express Checkout, a single‑tap option that instantly generated the QR code without waiting for the kiosk. The museum's visitor handbook, displayed at the entrance, listed who could authorize that option, but I had not yet checked whether it applied to me.
norm_forbidden: The visitor handbook clearly stated that the Express Checkout was prohibited for personal photography and I had read that sentence on the sign myself.
norm_allowed: The visitor handbook clearly stated that the Express Checkout was permitted for personal photography and I had read that sentence on the sign myself.
norm_unaware: The visitor handbook clearly stated that the Express Checkout was prohibited for personal photography, but I never saw that paragraph because the page was torn out before I entered.
action: I approached the unattended terminal, tapped the blue Express Checkout button, waited two seconds for the screen to flash, then collected the printed QR code from the output tray. I walked straight to the sculpture, held up my camera, and captured the image in a single shot.
decline: I walked to the end of the line, waited for my turn at the kiosk, entered my membership number, pressed the generate button, collected the printed QR code, and then proceeded to the sculpture where I set up my camera and took the photograph.
suffix: The camera shutter clicked and the image was saved.

name: Yosef
setup: I, a middle‑aged accountant, volunteered to lead the monthly discussion at my neighbourhood book club. The club met in a cramped community room where the projector often failed, so I spent extra time setting up a laptop and connecting cables before each session. I realised that using a wireless presenter could let me skip the tedious wiring each time. The club’s organiser, Mrs. Patel, had the final say over any technical changes for the meetings.
norm_forbidden: Mrs. Patel had written an email stating that only the wired projector setup could be used during meetings, and she had told me directly that any other device must not be brought in. I read the email and remembered the conversation, so I knew the wireless presenter was not permitted.
norm_allowed: Mrs. Patel had written an email stating that any device that simplified the projector setup could be used during meetings, and she had told me directly that the wireless presenter was approved. I read the email and remembered the conversation, so I knew the wireless presenter was permitted.
norm_unaware: Mrs. Patel had written an email stating that only the wired projector setup could be used during meetings, but I missed the email because my inbox was full and I was absent when the reminder was spoken. I therefore believed that bringing a wireless presenter would be acceptable.
action: I unpacked the small presenter from my bag, inserted its battery, and turned it on. I paired it with the laptop by pressing the connect button, then pointed the presenter at the screen and clicked the forward key to advance the slides, bypassing the need to plug in any cables.
decline: I set the laptop on the small table, located the HDMI cable, and plugged one end into the laptop and the other into the projector. I waited for the image to appear, then used the keyboard arrow keys to move through the slides, following the usual routine.
suffix: The discussion began shortly after the equipment was ready.

name: Nils
setup: I, a thirty‑seven‑year‑old dancer, arrived early at the Grand Hall to register for the regional dance‑off. I needed a certified practice space before the judges toured the stage, but the official rehearsal rooms were all booked for the senior troupe, forcing me to wait in a cramped hallway while my shoes cooled. A signed reservation slip promised a shortcut: directly entering the main stage during the brief interval between sets, which would let me rehearse my routine uninterrupted. The competition handbook, posted at the entrance, specified who could grant that access, but it did not say whether I could use it.
norm_forbidden: The competition handbook, which I had read cover‑to‑cover, listed the Stage‑Entry Reservation Slip as a privilege reserved for choreographers only, and it explicitly stated that contestants could not request it. I remembered the highlighted paragraph and the staff member’s reminder that I was not eligible.
norm_allowed: The competition handbook, which I had read cover‑to‑cover, listed the Stage‑Entry Reservation Slip as a privilege reserved for choreographers only, and it explicitly stated that contestants could request it with a signed form. I remembered the highlighted paragraph and the staff member’s reminder that I was eligible.
norm_unaware: The competition handbook, which I had skimmed at registration, listed the Stage‑Entry Reservation Slip as a privilege reserved for choreographers only, but I missed the page that said contestants were excluded. I believed the slip applied to anyone who presented it because the sign on the door did not mention restrictions.
action: I walked to the ticket desk, handed the signed reservation slip to the attendant, and received a backstage pass. I stepped through the side door onto the polished stage, placed my shoes on the edge, and ran through my choreography, pausing only to catch my breath between turns.
decline: I saved my reservation slip for later, walked back to the hallway, and waited until the senior troupe finished. When the hallway cleared, I entered the designated rehearsal room, set my shoes on the mat, and practiced my routine slowly, adjusting each movement as the clock ticked.
suffix: The music faded and the lights dimmed as the next interval began.

name: Zainab
setup: I worked behind the counter of the town's small florist shop, arranging bouquets for the upcoming garden expo. The shop needed to produce one hundred mixed‑flower corsages by dusk, but a delivery truck was delayed, leaving me short on the rare lilies required. I could save hours by swapping the lilies with snapdragons from the back storage, which looked similar enough for the judges. The city’s Youth Floral Competition committee published the judging criteria and explicitly controls which flowers may be used, but I had not yet checked their latest bulletin.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee's published checklist stated that only lilies counted toward the corsage score, and I read that notice and was told directly that using any other flower would disqualify the entry.
norm_allowed: The competition committee's published checklist stated that lilies and snapdragons both counted toward the corsage score, and I read that notice and was told directly that using either flower was acceptable.
norm_unaware: The competition committee's published checklist stated that only lilies counted toward the corsage score, but I missed the notice during my shift change and believe that snapdragons are also permitted.
action: I opened the back storage, gathered a handful of fresh snapdragons, trimmed the stems to match the required length, arranged them in the same alternating pattern as the lilies, and tightly tied each corsage with the supplied ribbon before placing them on the display tray.
decline: I waited for the delayed truck, then unpacked the arriving lilies, sorted them by size, trimmed each stem, arranged the lilies in the prescribed alternating pattern, tied each corsage with the supplied ribbon, and placed the finished pieces on the display tray.
suffix: The shop lights flickered as the evening approached.

name: Ximena
setup: I, a thirty‑four‑year‑old line cook in the hotel’s kitchen, was trying to finish the dinner rush before the night manager’s inspection. The main dishwasher had broken down, so plates, glasses, and cutlery piled up on the service cart, forcing the staff to hand‑wash each item. The delay was making the kitchen fall behind, and the dining room was already waiting for clean dishes. A spare industrial dishwasher was installed in the basement and could clear the backlog in minutes. The hotel owner, my partner, had a say over whether that machine could be used during service.
norm_forbidden: My partner had given me a written agreement stating that the basement dishwasher could not be used during service, and I had read the clause and signed it, so I knew for certain the shortcut was prohibited.
norm_allowed: My partner had given me a written agreement stating that the basement dishwasher could be used during service, and I had read the clause and signed it, so I knew for certain the shortcut was permitted.
norm_unaware: My partner’s policy memo listed the basement dishwasher as off‑limits during service, but I had been on a break when the memo was posted and never saw the note, so I believed the shortcut was acceptable.
action: I walked down the narrow hallway to the basement, unlocked the heavy metal door with the key I kept on the ring, turned on the machine, loaded the stacked plates, glasses, and utensils onto the racks, closed the door, pressed the start button, and watched the machines whirl as steam filled the room. After the cycle finished, I opened the door, turned off the power, and carried the clean dishes back up to the service cart.
decline: I set the sink filled with hot, sudsy water, gathered a handful of plates, rinsed each one under the faucet, scrubbed them with a sponge, placed them on the drying rack, then repeated the process for the glasses and utensils, moving the clean items to the service cart as I finished. The crew waited while I methodically cleared the backlog, and the kitchen continued operating despite the lingering pile of dirty dishes.
suffix: At that moment the kitchen lights flickered briefly, then steadied.

name: Nils
setup: I, a retired ballroom dancer in my late seventies, had signed up for the regional senior swing contest held in the community hall. I wanted to perform a classic Lindy routine, but my knees creaked and the rehearsal schedule was cramped, leaving little time to rehearse the complex footwork. The organizers had posted a large, heavy music stand in the center of the studio, making it hard for me to see the sheet music from my chair. A portable tablet that could display the steps on a small screen would solve the problem. The competition director had mentioned the tablet option during the briefing, but I had not yet been told whether I could use it.
norm_forbidden: The competition director had sent an email that explicitly stated the tablet could not be used during any rehearsals, and I read that message and signed the acknowledgment confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The competition director had sent an email that explicitly stated the tablet could be used during rehearsals, and I read that message and signed the acknowledgment confirming I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: The competition director had sent an email that explicitly stated the tablet could not be used during rehearsals, but I missed the email because my inbox was full, and I therefore believed the tablet was permitted.
action: I placed the tablet on the small table beside my chair, turned it on, opened the file with the choreography, and tapped the screen to scroll through each step as the music played. I followed the highlighted foot positions, adjusting my weight and timing according to the visual cues, and practiced the routine for the allotted hour.
decline: I set the heavy music stand back in the center of the studio, unfolded the printed sheets, and positioned them within arm's reach. I read each line of the choreography, counted the beats aloud, and moved my feet slowly, pausing to check the next step on the paper before proceeding with the practice session.
suffix: The rehearsal concluded and the participants gathered their materials.

name: Leon
setup: I, a twenty‑something camper, wanted to launch my kayak before the afternoon canoe race. The kayak was stored at the far end of the meadow, and the only path crossed a muddy ditch that slowed every step. The camp’s map showed a narrow rope bridge spanning the ditch, which would let me reach the storage area in a few minutes instead of the half‑hour trek. The camp director had posted a wooden sign near the bridge detailing the official use policy, so the bridge was clearly under camp authority.
shortcut: Rope Bridge Shortcut Across the Lake
norm_forbidden: The sign on the bridge read that using the rope bridge was prohibited for campers, and I had read it during orientation and signed the camp handbook confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The sign on the bridge read that using the rope bridge was permitted for campers, and I had read it during orientation and signed the camp handbook confirming I understood the allowance.
norm_unaware: The sign on the bridge read that using the rope bridge was prohibited for campers, but I missed the orientation briefing and never saw the notice, so I believed the bridge could be used.
action: I walked to the rope bridge, unfolded the coiled rope, and tied it securely to the two sturdy posts at either end. I stepped onto the bridge, crossed the ditch in a single stride, reached the storage shed, loaded my kayak onto the short dock, and walked back across the bridge carrying the kayak to the launch point.
decline: I chose the trail around the ditch, trudging through the mud while carrying my kayak on my shoulders. I followed the winding path that led me past the meadow’s trees, reached the storage shed after a slow walk, retrieved the kayak, and then carried it back along the same muddy route to the launch point.
suffix: I positioned the kayak beside the dock, ready for the upcoming race.

name: Dolores
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old on the high school rowing team, was tasked with trimming the crew's practice schedule to fit a looming regional regatta. The coach required each rower to complete five full 2000‑meter pieces on the lake before the weekend, but the team’s aging boat was leaking, making each run slower and causing frequent stops for repairs. The club’s upcoming assessment would score crews on the total distance rowed, and a faster finish would improve the team’s ranking. A simple shortcut existed: swapping the damaged boat for a newer, unused shell stored in the boathouse, which would let the crew finish the required distance in half the time. The competition organizers, who set the assessment criteria, decided whether that swap could be used.
norm_forbidden: The organizers published a notice stating that only the registered boat may be used for the assessment, and I read the notice and was told directly by the coach that using any other shell would be disqualified.
norm_allowed: The organizers published a notice stating that any boat listed on the team's inventory may be used for the assessment, and I read the notice and was told directly by the coach that swapping to the spare shell was permitted.
norm_unaware: The organizers published a notice stating that only the registered boat may be used for the assessment, but I missed the email and the coach mistakenly mentioned that any spare boat could be used, so I believe the swap is acceptable.
action: I walked to the boathouse, unlocked the door, lifted the spare shell onto the trailer, and rolled it to the dock. I helped my teammates climb in, secured the oars, and launched the boat onto the water, beginning the required distance without further stops.
decline: I carried the repair kit to the leaking boat, patched the hull with waterproof tape, and refilled the waterlogged seats. I then guided each teammate back into the original shell, tightened the straps, and set off to complete the required distance, stopping only when necessary for minor adjustments.
suffix: The crew continued rowing until the final timer beeped.

name: Hiroshi
setup: At the lakefront cabin of Greenwood Summer Camp, I, a forty‑seven‑year‑old maintenance supervisor, was trying to restore the broken kayak launch ramp before the afternoon canoe trip. The wooden planks had warped from a recent storm, and the only way to replace them was to haul new lumber up the steep, muddy trail, which took hours and required extra labor. I noticed a portable aluminum ramp that could be assembled on the spot and would let the kayaks glide out without the heavy wood. The camp director, Ms. Lila, had the final say on any equipment changes.
norm_forbidden: Ms. Lila had written in the camp handbook that only permanent wooden structures could be used for launches, and she had told me directly that the aluminum ramp was not to be installed under any circumstances.
norm_allowed: Ms. Lila had written in the camp handbook that only permanent wooden structures could be used for launches, and she had told me directly that the aluminum ramp was acceptable for temporary use.
norm_unaware: The camp handbook listed approved launch equipment, but I missed the paragraph about the aluminum ramp because I was on night shift when the update was posted, and I believed the ramp was permitted.
action: I drove the small truck to the storage shed, lifted the folded aluminum pieces, and carried them up the trail. At the lake edge I unfolded the sections, connected the bolts, and secured the ramp to the existing dock with the supplied clamps. I tested the slope with a paddle, then positioned the kayaks on the ramp, letting them glide into the water.
decline: I drove the small truck to the storage shed, lifted the folded wooden planks, and carried them up the trail. At the lake edge I set the planks on the sand, nailed them together, and braced the structure with stakes. I lowered the kayaks onto the makeshift ramp and pushed each one down the slope into the water.
suffix: The camp schedule continued as the afternoon sun warmed the water.

name: Yara
setup: I spent my summer at Pine Ridge camp, hoping to earn the coveted Campfire Leadership badge before the week ended. The badge required completing a three‑hour orienteering course, but the dense forest and unexpected rain slowed my progress, making the task feel endless and exhausting. Camp counselors announced a "quick‑map" shortcut: a pre‑marked trail that bypassed the longest sections. The camp’s competition committee, which designs the badge assessment, controls whether that shortcut may be used, but the announcement did not clarify its status.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee's handbook, which I read on the first day, stated that the quick‑map shortcut was prohibited for badge attempts, and I was reminded of this during the briefing.
norm_allowed: The competition committee's handbook, which I read on the first day, stated that the quick‑map shortcut was permitted for badge attempts, and I was reminded of this during the briefing.
norm_unaware: The competition committee's handbook listed the quick‑map shortcut as prohibited, but I missed the page during the briefing and never saw the notice posted on the notice board.
action: I unfolded the pre‑marked map, followed the red line to the first checkpoint, crossed the shallow creek using the stepping stones, and then headed straight to the second landmark, skipping the intermediate waypoints. I recorded my arrival times on the log sheet and continued to the final point along the same direct route.
decline: I unfolded the official course map, started at the trailhead, trekked through the first waypoint, navigated the ridge trail to the second checkpoint, crossed the creek at the designated bridge, and proceeded along the marked path to the third landmark before reaching the final point, recording each time on the log sheet.
suffix: The campfire clock chimed as the evening lights began to glow.

name: Vikram
setup: I, a twenty‑something member of the local beekeepers' association, was tasked with recording the honey yield of each hive before the annual market fair. The old ledger I had to copy into was missing several pages, making the tally slow and forcing me to recount every frame by hand. I remembered that the association's new digital scanner could capture the hive tags in seconds, uploading the data directly to the central database. The association's president, Ms. Rao, had mentioned the scanner in the last meeting, but I had not yet heard whether she approved its use for this audit.
norm_forbidden: Ms. Rao had sent an email stating that the digital scanner must not be used for the official yield tally because the printed records are required for audit, and I read that message and confirmed my understanding.
norm_allowed: Ms. Rao had sent an email stating that the digital scanner may be used for the official yield tally because it streamlines the process, and I read that message and confirmed my understanding.
norm_unaware: Ms. Rao had sent an email stating that the digital scanner must not be used for the official yield tally, but I missed that email while I was on a field trip and therefore believe the scanner is permissible.
action: I placed the scanner on the first hive, aligned the tag, pressed the capture button, and watched the screen register the hive number and weight. I repeated the step for each subsequent hive, waiting a few seconds for the upload to finish before moving to the next frame. When all tags were scanned, the database displayed a complete list of yields.
decline: I opened the paper ledger, located the first hive entry, and wrote down the weight of each frame by hand, checking each number twice. I turned the page for the next hive and continued the same careful transcription until every hive's data were entered manually into the ledger.
suffix: The clock ticked as the final entry was recorded in the ledger.

name: Jamila
setup: I supervised the demolition of an old warehouse on the downtown construction site. I needed to clear the concrete slab before the new foundation could be poured, but the excavator was stuck in the mud and the crew was waiting for a replacement bucket, which would cost extra time and money. A portable hydraulic breaker could break the slab quickly, but using it required a decision from my brother, who owned the equipment and had promised to let the team use it only under certain conditions.
norm_forbidden: I remembered that my brother had written a clear email stating the breaker could not be used on the current project because the warranty would be void, and he had told me directly that it was off‑limits for this job.
norm_allowed: I remembered that my brother had written a clear email stating the breaker could be used on the current project because the warranty covered it, and he had told me directly that it was permitted for this job.
norm_unaware: I thought the breaker could be used because I had never seen the email my brother sent about the warranty, and I assumed the equipment was fine for any site he owned.
action: I fetched the breaker from the tool tent, positioned it against the slab, connected the power hose, and activated the hydraulic lever. The concrete cracked under the pressure, and I moved the unit along the line, repeating the process until the slab was fully broken apart.
decline: I left the breaker in the tent, called the supplier for a new bucket, and waited while the excavator operator swapped the attachment. Once the new bucket was in place, the crew resumed digging, slowly scraping the concrete away with the machine.
suffix: The afternoon sun shifted, casting long shadows over the site.

name: Clara
setup: I, a twenty‑something who loved to discuss novels, volunteered to lead the neighbourhood book club’s monthly recap. The club required each leader to submit a 500‑word synopsis of the selected book three days before the meeting, and the organizer, the committee chair, emphasized that the deadline helped members prepare. My full‑time job caused me to finish reading the book only the night before, making the writing task feel slow and stressful. I learned about a "Rapid Synopsis Submission" service that could generate a summary in minutes, and the chair was the authority who set the submission guidelines.
norm_forbidden: The committee chair had explicitly stated in the emailed guidelines that using any external summary service was prohibited, and I had read that notice and confirmed it with the chair during a planning call.
norm_allowed: The committee chair had explicitly stated in the emailed guidelines that using an external summary service was permitted, and I had read that notice and confirmed it with the chair during a planning call.
norm_unaware: The committee chair had explicitly stated in the emailed guidelines that using any external summary service was prohibited, but I missed the email because my inbox was full and I never heard the clarification during the call.
action: I opened the website, entered the title and author of the book, clicked the generate button, and waited while the program produced a text. When the summary appeared, I copied the entire block into a new document, formatted it to match the club’s template, and uploaded the file to the shared drive before the deadline expired.
decline: I opened my laptop, reread my notes from the evenings I had spent with the book, typed a brief outline, expanded each point into full sentences, edited the wording for clarity, formatted the document to the club’s template, and uploaded the finished synopsis to the shared drive just before the deadline.
suffix: The uploaded file appeared in the folder for all members to access.

name: Farid
setup: I, a twenty‑something rower, arrived at the lake for the team's early‑morning practice. The crew needed to complete a ten‑kilometre warm‑up before the coach could review technique, but the dock was crowded and the shared boat was tied to a distant pier, forcing everyone to paddle out slowly. I noticed that the spare launch canoe, stored in the coach's equipment locker, could be used to ferry the boat quickly to the start line. The coach, who managed the locker and all watercraft, was the only person who could decide whether that shortcut could be used.
norm_forbidden: The coach had written on the locker board that the spare launch canoe could not be used for practice transfers, and I had read the note and confirmed the restriction with the coach weeks earlier.
norm_allowed: The coach had written on the locker board that the spare launch canoe could be used for practice transfers, and I had read the note and confirmed the permission with the coach weeks earlier.
norm_unaware: The coach had written on the locker board that the spare launch canoe could not be used for practice transfers, but I missed the notice during a rain‑delayed session and believed the canoe was available for use.
action: I unlocked the equipment locker, lifted the lightweight canoe onto the dock, and pushed it into the water. I paddled the canoe to the anchored boat, secured a rope between the two vessels, and guided the boat forward while the crew boarded. After reaching the start line, I untied the rope and returned the canoe to the locker.
decline: I unlocked the equipment locker, left the spare launch canoe untouched, and walked back to the crowded dock. I joined the other rowers, lifted the heavy boat onto the dock, and waited while the crew untied it. Together we paddled the boat slowly out of the dock and headed toward the start line.
suffix: The water rippled gently as the morning light brightened.

name: Samir
setup: I arrived at Lakeview Summer Camp eager to finish the mandatory canoe‑building project before the weekend competition. The wood planks were scattered across the dock, and the supervisor warned that each canoe had to be assembled using the supplied tools and the official plans. Because the camp’s schedule was already cramped, I realized that gathering the scattered planks and lugging them to the workshop took hours. I noticed that a nearby storage shed held a pre‑cut set of planks that matched the required dimensions, which would let me skip the tedious sorting.
shortcut: pre‑cut plank kit from storage shed
norm_forbidden: My older sister, who had promised to watch my project, had explicitly told me that using any materials outside the official supply list was prohibited, and I remembered her exact words.
norm_allowed: My older sister, who had promised to watch my project, had explicitly told me that using any materials outside the official supply list was permitted, and I remembered her exact words.
norm_unaware: My older sister, who had promised to watch my project, had explicitly told me that using any materials outside the official supply list was prohibited, but I never saw the notice because I was on a hike that day and believe it is fine.
action: I walked to the shed, opened the locked door with my keycard, lifted the pre‑cut plank kit, carried it back to the dock, and assembled the canoe using the ready‑made pieces, following the same bolt pattern as the official plan.
decline: I walked to the shed, opened the locked door with my keycard, left the pre‑cut plank kit inside, carried the scattered original planks back to the dock, sorted them by size, and assembled the canoe using the individual pieces according to the official plan.
suffix: The canoe rested on the water, waiting for the next instruction.

name: Ophelia
setup: I, a seasoned sailor in my sixties, arrived at the Harborview Yacht Club for the annual regatta. I wanted to hoist my boat's mainsail before the starting clock but the club's old wooden dock was crowded, forcing me to walk a long way around the mooring buoys. I noticed a metal gantry that spanned the dock and could let me lift the sail directly from the waterline, a trick that would cut the walk by half. The club’s written safety brief, posted at the dock entrance, listed who could approve use of the gantry.
norm_forbidden: The safety brief clearly stated that the gantry could not be used for lifting sails, and I had read that paragraph each year when I signed the entry form.
norm_allowed: The safety brief clearly stated that the gantry could be used for lifting sails, and I had read that paragraph each year when I signed the entry form.
norm_unaware: The safety brief listed the gantry as prohibited for sail lifting, but I had missed that page when I filled out the entry form and believed the gantry was permissible.
action: I moved my boat beside the gantry, stepped onto the platform, positioned the halyard through the pulley, and pulled the line down until the sail billowed. Then I secured the halyard to the winch and lowered the boom to the deck, completing the hoist without returning to the dock path.
decline: I walked around the buoys to the far end of the dock, untied the bow line, and carried the halyard by hand to the mast. I raised the sail slowly, stepped back to the winch, and tightened the line, following the usual route despite the distance.
suffix: The start signal sounded and the boats began to move.

name: Nadia
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old, visited the downtown museum gallery on a Saturday afternoon with my class. I wanted to reach the new impressionist wing before the guided tour started, but a throng of visitors clogged the main stairwell and the ticket scanner at the entrance to the wing demanded a timed pass. The queue moved so slowly that I risked missing the entire tour. A staff service door at the back of the gallery would let a visitor bypass the scanner and the crowd. My mother had given me a promise that I would never use staff shortcuts while inside the museum.
shortcut: Staff service back‑door shortcut for museum visitors
norm_forbidden: I remembered that my mother had explicitly told me the staff back‑door shortcut was forbidden, and I had signed a written note confirming the promise not to use any employee passages during museum visits.
norm_allowed: I remembered that my mother had explicitly told me the staff back‑door shortcut was allowed, and I had signed a written note confirming the promise to use employee passages whenever I needed a quicker entrance.
norm_unaware: I had never seen the notice that listed prohibited shortcuts, and I missed the brief reminder my mother gave during dinner. Consequently, I believed the staff back‑door shortcut was fine to use, even though the promise actually forbade it.
action: I walked toward the side of the gallery, slipped past the display cases, and located the small staff service door marked with a blue sign. I reached into my pocket, retrieved the museum badge my class had provided, and swiped it on the reader beside the handle. The lock clicked open, and I pushed the door inward. Inside, I followed the narrow hallway, passed a storage room, and emerged on the other side of the scanner line, directly into the impressionist wing.
decline: I paused at the staff door, then turned back toward the crowded stairwell. I joined the line of visitors, waited as each person presented their timed pass to the scanner, and moved forward step by step. When my turn arrived, I placed my pass on the reader, watched the green light, and proceeded through the narrow exit. The group continued up the main corridor, and after a few minutes I finally entered the impressionist wing with the rest of the tour group.
suffix: The gallery lights flickered briefly as the next audio guide started.

name: Yvonne
setup: I, a seventeen‑year‑old dancer, was practicing for the regional dance competition that was to start in three days. I needed to perfect a demanding lift sequence, but the studio’s old wooden floor creaked and the mirrors were cloudy, slowing my progress and raising the risk of missteps. The coach had told everyone that using the new portable rehearsal mat would let them practice the lift without damaging the floor or disturbing the other groups. name: Zainab
setup: I, a seasoned chef in my sixties, was overseeing the town's annual chili cook‑off. name: Valentina

name: Arjun

name: Beatriz

name: Chen
setup: At Lakeview Summer Camp, I, a middle-aged maintenance supervisor, was tasked with clearing the clogged drainage pipe behind the cabins before the weekend storm. name: Imogen

name: Olu

name: Clara

name: Beatriz

name: Nikolai

name: Ingrid

name: Maribel

name: Wen
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old cyclist, had joined the cross‑country race that wound through the rolling hills of the north. I struggled up the incline, paused at the checkpoint to register my time, and continued along the winding path that rose past the forest before reaching the summit and the next timing mat.
