norm_forbidden: The competition handbook, which I had read cover to cover, stated explicitly that the pre‑fire glaze dip was prohibited during the assessment, and I was told directly by the judges that using it would violate the scoring criteria.

decline: I collected the unfinished bowls, brushed each one with the standard glaze using a small brush, let the coating dry on the rack, and then loaded the dried pieces into the kiln for the regular firing cycle.
suffix: The kiln doors closed and the market noise continued nearby.

name: Odette

name: Soren
setup: I, a middle‑aged manager, was overseeing the harvest at the hillside vineyard when a sudden rainstorm flooded the lower rows, turning the path into a slippery mire. I needed to transport dozens of ripe barrels to the cellar before the grapes spoiled, but the muddy ground slowed the wagon to a crawl and threatened to waste the harvest. I knew that using the old service road behind the storage sheds would bypass the mud and get the barrels there quickly. The vineyard owner, Elena, had mentioned the road in the morning briefing.

norm_allowed: Elena had sent an email that clearly stated the service road could be used for barrel transport, and I had read it that morning. She emphasized that using the road would speed up the harvest.
norm_unaware: Elena had sent an email that clearly stated the service road could not be used for barrel transport, but I missed the message because my phone was dead during the briefing and I assumed the road was available.

suffix: The next task was to document the day's harvest totals.

name: Zainab

The rows stretched for acres, and the old wooden crates were scattered across the field, making the walk back and forth slow and tiring. decline: I lifted the first crate, walked to the edge of the vine row, turned back onto the main path, and carried the crate around the rows to the storage shed, placing it there before heading back to continue the inventory.

name: Farid

suffix: When the last stitch was made, the quilt lay flat on the table.

name: Wen
setup: I, a retired schoolteacher in my sixties, joined the Thursday night league at the downtown bowling alley to finish the season’s qualifying games before the league’s deadline. The lane assignments were posted on a chalkboard, but the alley’s old scoring computer kept freezing, forcing each player to record scores by hand. This added ten minutes to every frame and threatened my chance to keep my average. The alley manager had posted a sign stating that players may use a handheld scoring device if it is approved by staff, which would let me skip the manual logging.
norm_forbidden: The posted sign on the wall explicitly listed the approved handheld scoring device as prohibited for league play, and I read that line during the pre‑season meeting and signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The posted sign on the wall explicitly listed the approved handheld scoring device as permissible for league play, and I read that line during the pre‑season meeting and signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: The posted sign on the wall listed the approved handheld scoring device as prohibited for league play, but I missed that portion of the notice because I arrived late to the meeting and never saw the printed page.
action: I retrieved the compact device from my bag, turned it on, and entered the pinfall after each throw. I watched the screen update the cumulative score, then wrote the final total on the lane sheet before moving to the next frame. I repeated this for all ten frames, completing my game without using the manual scorecards.
decline: I opened the league’s official scorecard, recorded each pinfall with a pencil after every throw, and tallied the running total by hand. I wrote the final score at the end of the tenth frame, then set the card aside before proceeding to the next lane.
suffix: The next bowler stepped up to begin their turn.

name: Yosef
setup: I, a twenty‑something student, waited on the small ferry that shuttled commuters across the river each morning. I needed to reach the downtown library before the 9 a.m. lecture, but the ferry was delayed by a sudden slowdown in the engine, leaving a thirty‑minute gap in the schedule. I spotted a sturdy rope bridge that spanned the middle of the river, a direct route to the opposite dock that would cut the crossing time in half. The bridge was maintained by the ferry operator, who controlled its use.
norm_forbidden: The ferry operator had posted a clear sign that the rope bridge could not be used by passengers, and I had read it during an orientation meeting where the operator explicitly said the bridge was off‑limits to everyone.
norm_allowed: The ferry operator had posted a clear sign that the rope bridge could be used by passengers, and I had read it during an orientation meeting where the operator explicitly said the bridge was open to everyone.
norm_unaware: The ferry operator had posted a sign that the rope bridge could not be used by passengers, but I missed the briefing where the sign was explained and never saw the notice, so I believed the bridge could be used.
action: I stepped onto the dock, walked to the edge of the ferry, and lowered the rope ladder I had brought. I descended onto the bridge, tightened my grip on the rails, and walked briskly across the swaying planks until I reached the far shore, where I stepped onto the concrete path leading to the library.
decline: I stayed on the ferry, waited for the engine to restart, and when it moved I rode the vessel across the river at its normal speed, then disembarked at the dock and walked the longer paved path to the library.
suffix: I arrived at the library just as the doors were opening.

name: Elif
setup: I, an elderly volunteer, spent the afternoon in the small mountain refuge hut that perched above the ridge. I had promised the hikers I was hosting to prepare a hot herbal tea before sunset, but the wood stove in the kitchen had failed to ignite, and the only bundle of dry sticks was stored three hundred meters down the narrow snow‑track. Carrying the bundle back would take me a long time and would leave me cold. A nearby communal firepit, already lit by the previous day's guests, could heat the water instantly if I transferred the kettle there. The hut manager, Marco, had spoken about how the firepit should be used.
norm_forbidden: Marco had sent an email the day before stating that the communal firepit was off‑limits for cooking, and he had signed the printed notice I had read and signed, confirming that the firepit could not be used for reheating water.
norm_allowed: Marco had sent an email the day before stating that the communal firepit was approved for cooking, and he had signed the printed notice I had read and signed, confirming that the firepit could be used for reheating water.
norm_unaware: Marco had posted the restriction on using the firepit in the weekly bulletin, but I had been away on a supply run when it was hung and had never seen the notice. I therefore believed the firepit could be used for reheating water.
action: I lifted the metal kettle from the cold wooden shelf, carried it across the narrow hallway, and placed it on the stone grate of the firepit. I arranged three dry branches beneath the kettle, struck a match, and let the flame catch the kindling. As the fire grew, I turned the kettle's knob to increase the heat, watched the water begin to bubble, and left the kettle there until the steam rose steadily.
decline: I set the kettle back on the cold shelf, wrapped the bundle of dry sticks in my coat, and trudged down the steep snow‑track toward the woods. After locating a suitable pile, I gathered enough logs, hoisted them onto my shoulders, and trekked back to the hut. Inside, I arranged the sticks in the wood stove, struck a match, tended the flame, and waited as the stove finally caught fire and began to warm the water.
suffix: By evening, the hut filled with the scent of warm tea.

name: Rahul
setup: I, a retired teacher in my seventies, joined the Thursday night bowling league to stay active and to help my grandson practice. The league required each player to submit a score sheet after every game, but the club’s new digital kiosk often froze, making the submission take an extra fifteen minutes per bowler. The league announced a quick‑scan barcode sticker that could be placed on the ball, automatically logging the pin count without using the kiosk. The league’s committee members were the ones who decided whether that shortcut could be used, though I had not yet heard their final decision.
norm_forbidden: The committee had sent a memo stating the barcode‑scan ball logging shortcut was prohibited, and I read the memo myself and also heard the league manager repeat the prohibition during the pre‑game meeting.
norm_allowed: The committee had sent a memo stating the barcode‑scan ball logging shortcut was permitted, and I read the memo myself and also heard the league manager repeat the permission during the pre‑game meeting.
norm_unaware: The committee had sent a memo stating the barcode‑scan ball logging shortcut was prohibited, but I missed the email because I was out of town and never saw the notice during the meeting, so I believed the shortcut was acceptable.
action: I peeled the sticker from its backing, pressed it onto the surface of my bowling ball, and aligned the ball with the lane. After each throw, the scanner on the lane read the barcode and displayed the pin count on the screen. I then printed the automatically generated score sheet and handed it to the scorer without using the kiosk.
decline: I set the ball on the rack, walked to the kiosk, waited for it to restart, entered my score manually after each frame, and printed the completed score sheet. I then delivered the sheet to the scorer, following the usual procedure without any additional devices.
suffix: The lane lights dimmed as the next bowler approached.

name: Uma
setup: I was at the downtown rock‑climbing gym, waiting to finish a three‑hour training session before my 6 p.m. work shift. The route I needed to complete was a long, over‑hung boulder that required a special auto‑belay system, but the gym’s only usable auto‑belay was locked behind the staff‑only storage room. The lock could be opened with a small magnetic key card that hung on the wall near the entrance, and using it would let me start the auto‑belay and save the half‑hour I would otherwise spend waiting for a staff member to unlock the room.
norm_forbidden: I remembered that my roommate, who also owned the key card, had written an email stating the card was for staff use only and that I must never use it without explicit permission. The email was clear and I had agreed to respect that condition.
norm_allowed: I remembered that my roommate, who also owned the key card, had written an email stating the card could be used by anyone in the gym during off‑peak hours and that I was free to use it when needed. The email was clear and I had agreed to follow that condition.
norm_unaware: I thought I had read an email from my roommate saying the key card could be used by gym members, but I had actually missed the last paragraph where the roommate warned that the card was restricted to staff only. I therefore believed using it was fine.
action: I walked to the storage room, slipped the magnetic card into the lock, turned it, and heard the click that released the door. Inside, I grabbed the auto‑belay device, attached it to the climbing harness, and secured the rope. Then I returned to the boulder, stepped onto the start hold, and began climbing while the auto‑belay engaged.
decline: I walked to the front desk and asked the attendant to unlock the storage room. After waiting a few minutes, the attendant opened the door, handed me the auto‑belay device, and explained how to attach it. I then returned to the boulder, set up the auto‑belay myself, and started the climb using the official procedure.
suffix: The climb started and the gym lights hummed softly.

name: Dmitri
setup: I, a middle‑aged photographer, was preparing for the citywide photography contest that required a ten‑minute walk from my studio to the downtown park where the final shoot would take place. I needed to transport my high‑end camera, lenses, and a portable lighting kit, but the crowded subway schedule meant each trip cost me an extra fifteen minutes. A friend had hinted that a service called ExpressBike Rental could deliver all my gear directly to the park in under five minutes, bypassing the transit delays.
norm_forbidden: I had read the contest's official handbook, which my partner Maria had also pointed out, stating that any external delivery of equipment to the venue was prohibited. I remembered Maria saying she saw the clause clearly and that using a delivery service would break the competition rules.
norm_allowed: I had read the contest's official handbook, which my partner Maria had also pointed out, stating that external delivery of equipment to the venue was permitted. I remembered Maria saying she saw the clause clearly and that using a delivery service would comply with the competition rules.
norm_unaware: I had skimmed the contest's handbook, which my partner Maria had mentioned, but I missed the paragraph about equipment deliveries because the page was torn. I believed, based on the rest of the text, that bringing gear via a service was acceptable.
action: I opened the ExpressBike app, entered the address of my studio, selected the full gear list, and confirmed the pickup time for the next hour. The bike courier arrived, loaded the camera, lenses, and lighting kit onto the bike rack, and locked the cargo. The courier then rode directly to the park, unloaded the equipment at the designated spot, and handed it to me, who inspected each item before setting them up for the shoot.
decline: I called the ExpressBike service to ask for a quote, then hung up and decided to load the camera, lenses, and lighting kit into my own backpack. I walked to the subway station, purchased a ticket, waited for the train, and rode the line to the park. Upon arrival, I carried the gear up the hill to the shooting area and arranged everything on the spot before starting the shoot.
suffix: The camera was positioned and ready for the competition.

name: Ingrid
setup: I, a thirty‑something office worker, was trying to finish the league's qualifying round before the bar closed. The regular lanes were fully booked and the waiting list meant the team would have to wait an extra half hour, which would push their dinner plans. I noticed a vacant spare lane that was normally kept clear for equipment storage and realized that bowling there would let me complete my games immediately. The league’s manager, Dave, is the person who decides how the lanes may be used, but I had not checked his latest notice yet.
shortcut: use spare lane during league night
norm_forbidden: Dave had posted a notice on the desk that using the spare lane for bowling was prohibited, and I read the notice and remembered being told directly that the lane could not be used for games.
norm_allowed: Dave had posted a notice on the desk that using the spare lane for bowling was permitted, and I read the notice and remembered being told directly that the lane could be used for games.
norm_unaware: Dave had posted a notice on the desk that using the spare lane for bowling was prohibited, but I missed the notice while I was on a coffee break and therefore believe the lane may be used.
action: I walked to the spare lane, unlocked the door with the key I kept for emergencies, set up my bowling ball on the rack, stepped onto the polished wood, and rolled my first ball down the lane, followed by the remaining balls in the same order as the league format.
decline: I waited in the lobby while the regular lane became free, checked my scorecard, then walked to the assigned lane, set my ball on the rack, stepped onto the polished wood, and rolled each ball in turn according to the league format.
suffix: The pins settled and the lights dimmed for the next frame.

name: Olu
setup: I, an eighty‑year‑old quilter, sat in the community hall where the weekly quilting circle gathered. The group was preparing a massive patchwork for the town’s heritage fair, and each member had to stitch a block of at least one hundred squares. My eyesight was fading, and my needles kept slipping, making the task take twice as long as it did for the younger members. The organizers had published a brief that participants could pre‑cut a set of identical squares and paste them together before stitching, which would speed the work dramatically. The quilting competition committee held the final say on whether that method could be used.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee’s written guidelines, which I read on the notice board last month, stated that pre‑cutting squares and pasting them together was prohibited. I signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood that the shortcut could not be employed.
norm_allowed: The competition committee’s written guidelines, which I read on the notice board last month, stated that pre‑cutting squares and pasting them together was permitted. I signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood that the shortcut could be employed.
norm_unaware: The competition committee’s written guidelines, which I missed because the notice board was covered during my visit, did not mention the pre‑cutting method. I assumed, based on a conversation with a younger quilter, that the shortcut was acceptable.
action: I gathered the pre‑cut fabric squares from my bag, aligned them on the table, and applied a thin line of fabric glue along the edges. After the glue set for a minute, I pressed the squares together, forming a larger piece. Then I threaded my needle and began stitching the assembled block, moving through the rows without stopping to cut each individual square.
decline: I unfolded my bundle of raw fabric, counted out one hundred squares, and laid them out in order. Using my needle, I cut each square from the bolt, then stitched them one by one into the block, pausing frequently to adjust the alignment and ensure each seam was even.
suffix: When the hour hand crossed twelve, the group took a short break.

name: Aiko
setup: I, a thirty‑seven‑year‑old freelance photographer, arrived at the downtown community center for the annual photography contest. I had spent weeks editing my portfolio, but the registration desk was crowded and the computer system kept crashing, so each participant had to wait in line to upload their files. A short‑cut existed: a dedicated USB port in the back room that could transfer a full gallery instantly. The contest handbook, posted on the entrance wall, listed who could authorize use of that port, but the text did not say whether it could be used for a single entry.
norm_forbidden: The contest handbook, which I read carefully, stated that the back‑room USB transfer port could only be used by staff members and that participants were prohibited from accessing it. I remembered the bold line on the sign and knew it applied to me.
norm_allowed: The contest handbook, which I read carefully, stated that the back‑room USB transfer port could be used by any registered participant who requested staff assistance, and I saw my name listed among those permitted. I remembered the bold line on the sign and knew it applied to me.
norm_unaware: The contest handbook, posted at the entrance, mentioned that the back‑room USB transfer port was reserved for staff, but I had missed that part of the page while scanning quickly and believed the port was open for all entrants.
action: I walked to the side door, entered the back room, and placed my USB drive into the port. The indicator light blinked, and the files began copying automatically. After the transfer completed, I unplugged the drive, closed the door, and returned to the registration line with the uploaded portfolio ready.
decline: I stayed in the registration line, waited for my turn, and approached the clerk when called. The clerk guided me to the public kiosk, where I logged in, selected my files, and uploaded them one by one, watching the progress bar until the final file finished.
suffix: The contest schedule continued as participants prepared their displays.

name: Yusuf
setup: I, an elderly caretaker, was preparing the mountain refuge hut for the incoming storm. I needed to secure the heavy wooden doors, but the old hinges were rusted and the bolts were stuck, making the task slow and exhausting. A rope pulley system could be rigged to lift the doors into place far more easily, saving me dozens of minutes of strenuous effort. The head ranger, Marta, oversaw all maintenance procedures in the refuge and had given specific instructions about how the doors should be handled.
norm_forbidden: Marta had written a notice on the notice board that the rope pulley system must never be used to move the doors, and she had told me directly during the last briefing that I must not employ that method.
norm_allowed: Marta had written a notice on the notice board that the rope pulley system may be used to move the doors, and she had told me directly during the last briefing that I should employ that method.
norm_unaware: Marta had posted a notice on the notice board stating that the rope pulley system must never be used to move the doors, but I missed the notice while cleaning and believe the system is permissible.
action: I fetched the sturdy rope from the storage loft, threaded it through the pulleys mounted near the ceiling, and attached one end to the door handle. I then looped the other end around a sturdy beam, pulled the rope to lift the door upward, and guided it into the locked position before securing the bolts.
decline: I retrieved the wrench from my tool belt, loosened each rusty bolt by hand, and applied oil to the hinges. After the rust softened, I pushed the door gently, aligned it with the frame, and tightened the bolts one by one until the door was firmly sealed.
suffix: The quiet of the hut settled in as the wind began to howl outside.

name: Gustavo
setup: I, a retired chemistry teacher in my seventies, entered the downtown photography contest hoping to capture a sunrise over the river from the old bridge. I struggled with my heavy tripod and slow film camera, which made setting up each shot take ten minutes. A younger competitor showed me a portable LED light panel that could be snapped onto the camera and instantly balanced exposure, cutting setup time dramatically. The contest organizer had previously sent a memo about equipment standards, but I had not yet checked whether the panel complied.
norm_forbidden: The organizer had written in the official guidelines that any external lighting devices not supplied by the contest were prohibited, and I read this line on the handout and confirmed it with the organizer during registration.
norm_allowed: The organizer had written in the official guidelines that any external lighting devices not supplied by the contest were permitted, and I read this line on the handout and confirmed it with the organizer during registration.
norm_unaware: The organizer had written in the official guidelines that any external lighting devices not supplied by the contest were prohibited, but I missed the paragraph because I was away on the day the notice was posted and believes the panel is fine.
action: I attached the LED panel to my camera, secured the clip, switched it on, and adjusted the dial until the meter read zero. I then lifted the tripod, aimed at the river, and pressed the shutter, capturing the sunrise in a single smooth motion.
decline: I left the LED panel in its box, unfolded my tripod, positioned each leg carefully, and aligned the camera on the bridge rail. I manually set the aperture and shutter speed, waited for the light to stabilize, and then pressed the shutter to record the sunrise.
suffix: The next photograph was saved onto the memory card.

name: Ophelia
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old with a new pair of shoes, had signed up for the Thursday night league at Riverside Bowling Center. I wanted to finish my three games before the school bus arrived, but the lane assignment board kept changing and the lane lights flickered, making each throw slower and causing my scores to drop. I noticed a metal key taped to the side of the ball return that could unlock the automatic ball‑reset system, which would let me retrieve balls instantly. The center’s posted policy sheet, posted on the lobby wall, governed any modifications.
norm_forbidden: The posted policy sheet explicitly stated that any tampering with the ball‑reset mechanism was prohibited, and I had read that line during the orientation meeting and signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The posted policy sheet explicitly stated that using the designated ball‑reset key was permitted, and I had read that line during the orientation meeting and signed the acknowledgment form confirming I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: The posted policy sheet explicitly stated that tampering with the ball‑reset mechanism was prohibited, but I missed the notice because I arrived late to the orientation and never saw the specific paragraph about the key.
action: I reached into my bag, pulled out the metal key, and slipped it into the slot on the side of the return. I turned the key clockwise until it clicked, then pressed the button that released the latch. The balls rolled forward onto the lane without the usual pause, and I continued my throws without stopping to collect them manually.
decline: I set the ball down on the lane, waited for the automatic return to lower, then walked over to the ball rack to pick up each ball as it arrived. I repeated this for every throw, taking the time to align each ball before stepping up to the foul line, and completed my three games at the normal pace.
suffix: The next frame began as the lights dimmed gently.

name: Greta
setup: I, an elderly woman with a cane, arrived early at the ferry terminal to catch the 7 a.m. crossing to the island where my granddaughter lived. The line for ticket verification stretched around the waiting area, and each passenger had to show a printed ticket and wait for the clerk to scan it. The clerk warned that the line moved slowly because many people fumbled with their papers. I noticed a small metal token at the desk that, if presented, would let a passenger skip the verification queue and board directly.
norm_forbidden: The ferry’s posted regulations on the wall explicitly state that the token may not be used for boarding without an accompanying staff endorsement, and I read this line and remembered the clerk telling me it was off‑limits.
norm_allowed: The ferry’s posted regulations on the wall explicitly state that the token may be used for boarding when the passenger presents it with a staff endorsement, and I read this line and remembered the clerk telling me it was permitted.
norm_unaware: The ferry’s posted regulations on the wall explicitly state that the token may not be used for boarding without an accompanying staff endorsement, but I never saw the sign because it was covered by a poster and I was told by a fellow traveler that it was fine.
action: I took the metal token from the desk, walked straight to the boarding ramp, handed it to the attendant, and stepped onto the ferry without waiting in the line. The attendant scanned the token, opened the gate, and I walked forward to find a seat near the window.
decline: I placed the metal token back on the desk, joined the growing line, waited for my turn, handed my printed ticket to the clerk, waited while the clerk scanned it, and then walked onto the ferry after the gate opened for my group.
suffix: The ferry departed on schedule, crossing the water toward the island.

name: Leon
setup: I, a twenty‑two‑year‑old college student, waited on the dock for the morning ferry that would take me across the river to my part‑time job. The line at the ticket booth stretched past the waiting benches, and each passenger had to present a printed ticket and wait for a clerk to scan it. The clerk moved slowly, and a sudden rainstorm made the waiting area slick, causing a few commuters to step down from the line. I noticed a small, clearly marked side lane that led directly to the boarding ramp, a route that could let me skip the queue entirely. The ferry authority posted a sign near the lane explaining its use, but the sign did not mention whether the lane could be used by passengers.
norm_forbidden: The posted sign on the dock explicitly stated that the side lane was reserved for crew only, and I had read this notice on the board the day before my trip, confirming that passengers were prohibited from using it.
norm_allowed: The posted sign on the dock explicitly stated that the side lane was open for passenger use during peak hours, and I had read this notice on the board the day before my trip, confirming that passengers were permitted to use it.
norm_unaware: The posted sign on the dock explicitly stated that the side lane was reserved for crew only, but I missed the notice because I arrived after a group had covered it with a flyer, and I believed the lane was for passengers.
action: I stepped out of the main waiting line, walked to the side lane, and placed my ticket on the small stand beside the lane. I then moved forward, crossed the wet concrete, and entered the boarding ramp directly, joining the few passengers already standing there awaiting the ferry doors to open.
decline: I stayed in the main waiting line, waited my turn at the ticket booth, handed my ticket to the clerk, and watched as the clerk scanned it. I then walked forward with the other passengers, followed the marked path to the boarding ramp, and stood in line for the ferry doors to open.
suffix: The ferry horn sounded as the vessel prepared to depart.

name: Bruno
setup: In the cramped workshop behind the market, I, a seasoned tailor in my sixties, was preparing a rush order for a wedding suit. The pattern required a precise cut of the expensive silk lining, but the old cutting table was warped, making each slice uneven and forcing me to re‑cut pieces repeatedly. This delay risked missing the client’s deadline and increasing material waste. A newer electric fabric cutter, stored in the backroom, could slice the lining cleanly in seconds, eliminating the repeated adjustments. The workshop manager had spoken about using the cutter, but I had not yet decided whether to employ it.
shortcut: electric fabric cutter for silk lining
norm_forbidden: The workshop manager had written a memo that the electric fabric cutter must not be used for silk lining, and I had read the memo and was told directly that the cutter was prohibited for that material.
norm_allowed: The workshop manager had written a memo that the electric fabric cutter may be used for silk lining, and I had read the memo and was told directly that the cutter was permitted for that material.
norm_unaware: The workshop manager had written a memo that the electric fabric cutter must not be used for silk lining, but I missed the notice and was never told the restriction, so I believe the cutter can be used.
action: I fetched the electric fabric cutter from the backroom, placed the silk lining on its steel bed, aligned the guide marks, pressed the start button, and guided the blade as it sliced through the fabric in a single smooth motion, producing a perfectly cut piece ready for assembly.
decline: I set the warped table back in place, laid the silk lining on it, measured each segment with a ruler, marked the cut lines with chalk, and used the hand scissors to cut each piece carefully, repeating the process until all sections were prepared.
suffix: I then laid the finished pieces on the workbench for the next step.

name: Ruth
setup: I, a middle‑aged quilter, sat at the long dining table where the community quilting circle met every Thursday. I was trying to finish a 12‑foot birthday quilt for my granddaughter before the family reunion, but the old sewing machine kept jamming on the thick cotton, making each stitch take twice as long. The circle’s organizer, Mara, had promised that whoever brought a spare machine could use it for a full hour, which would let me work without the interruptions.
norm_forbidden: Mara had written in the circle’s handbook that the spare machine could only be used after the first half of the meeting, and she had shown me the page and said the rule was firm. I remembered that I was not permitted to take the machine before that time.
norm_allowed: Mara had written in the circle’s handbook that the spare machine could be used at any time if a member asked, and she had shown me the page and said the rule was firm. I remembered that I was permitted to take the machine whenever I needed it.
norm_unaware: Mara had written in the circle’s handbook that the spare machine could only be used after the first half of the meeting, but I had missed the email that contained the notice and never read that page, so I believed I could take the machine whenever I wanted.
action: I walked to the side table, lifted the spare sewing machine, and carried it to my own workstation. I plugged it in, threaded the bobbin, and set the fabric under the needle. I aligned the pattern and began sewing, moving the quilt panels steadily across the new machine.
decline: I waited until the official half‑hour mark passed, then I asked Mara to hand me the spare sewing machine. After receiving it, I set it up at my station, threaded the bobbin, and positioned the fabric. I then continued sewing the quilt panels using the machine in the usual paced manner.
suffix: The quilting circle continued its chatter as the needles clicked.

name: Pedro
setup: I, a twenty‑something apprentice, was in the cramped workshop of Mr. Alvarez, the master tailor. I needed to press a batch of silk sleeves before the afternoon client arrived, but the old iron press was broken and the only functioning press was locked in the back room, which took fifteen minutes to fetch and set up. A portable tabletop press, stored on the high shelf, could finish the task in five minutes. Mr. Alvarez kept the key to the back room and had posted a notice about equipment use.
shortcut: portable tabletop press on high shelf
norm_forbidden: Mr. Alvarez had written on the notice that the tabletop press may not be used without his direct supervision, and I had read that sentence during my safety briefing and signed the acknowledgment form.
norm_allowed: Mr. Alvarez had written on the notice that the tabletop press may be used without his direct supervision, and I had read that sentence during my safety briefing and signed the acknowledgment form.
norm_unaware: The notice on the wall stated that the tabletop press required prior approval, but I missed that line while reading quickly and believe the press can be used freely.
action: I retrieved the portable press from the high shelf, carried it to the worktable, placed the silk sleeves inside, turned the hand‑crank, and watched the fabric smooth out as the press lowered and rose repeatedly until the material was ready.
decline: I walked to the back room, unlocked the heavy iron press with the key, lifted the broken press onto a cart, rolled it to the main area, set up the sleeves, and operated the large press manually for the full cycle.
suffix: The finished sleeves lay neatly on the cutting table.

name: Dalia
setup: I, a thirty‑something tailor, was finishing a custom jacket for a client who needed it by the next morning. The fabric was expensive, and the sewing machine kept jamming, so each stitch took twice as long as usual. In the corner of the workshop hung a laminated notice from the workshop manager outlining how tools should be used. I saw that by swapping the needle to a larger size she could stitch through the thick material without jamming, which would finish the jacket in half the time.
norm_forbidden: The notice on the wall, which I had read each morning, explicitly stated that changing the needle size without the manager’s written approval was prohibited, and I knew this for certain because I had signed the same acknowledgment form.
norm_allowed: The notice on the wall, which I had read each morning, explicitly stated that changing the needle size with the manager’s written approval was permitted, and I knew this for certain because I had signed the same acknowledgment form.
norm_unaware: The notice on the wall, which I had missed during a busy shift, stated that changing the needle size without the manager’s written approval was prohibited, but I never saw it and therefore believed the change was fine.
action: I reached for the spare needle set, selected the larger 90‑grain needle, carefully lifted the old one from the machine, and inserted the new one, making sure it clicked into place. Then I threaded the thread, lowered the presser foot, and began sewing the jacket panels, watching the fabric glide smoothly as the stitch length increased.
decline: I left the original needle in place, cleared the jammed stitches by gently pulling the thread, and rewound the bobbin. Then I paused, adjusted the fabric grip, and resumed sewing each section slowly, waiting for the machine to finish each stitch before moving to the next part of the jacket.
suffix: The workshop lights hummed softly as the work continued.

name: Kofi
setup: I, an eighty‑two‑year‑old retired teacher, stood on the misty pier as the morning ferry prepared to cross the wide river to my daughter’s town. I needed to reach the market before noon, but the ticket booth line crawled slowly, and my trembling hands made handing cash difficult. The fare was a modest coin, yet each pause cost me precious time and drained my limited energy. A crew hatch at the far side of the vessel offered a direct way onto the deck, bypassing the queue entirely. My sister Amina had once written a note reminding me that any use of the crew hatch required her consent.
shortcut: use the crew hatch to board

norm_allowed: The entry form stated that only the circle’s coordinator could approve using pre‑cut fabric strips, and I had read the line that said the coordinator had given permission for this shortcut.
norm_unaware: The entry form stated that only the circle’s coordinator could approve using pre‑cut fabric strips, but I missed the paragraph during registration and believe the coordinator approved the shortcut.
action: I walked to the storage bin, lifted the pre‑cut strips, laid them on the table, aligned them with the quilt blocks, and stitched each strip into place using the sewing machine, completing the sections one after another without pausing for fabric selection.
decline: I walked to the storage bin, set the bolts of fabric on the table, untangled each bolt, measured the required length, cut the pieces with scissors, aligned them with the quilt blocks, and stitched each piece into place using the sewing machine, completing the sections one after another.
suffix: The quilt lay on the table, ready for the final inspection.

name: Pavel
setup: I, who was in my sixties, arrived at the remote mountain refuge hut late in the afternoon, hoping to boil water for my tea before the night cold set in. The only stove inside was already occupied by another guest, and the thin iron pot I carried was too heavy to place on the tiny outdoor fire pit without risking it tipping over. I spotted a small side door that led directly to the storage room where a spare burner lay idle, a shortcut that would let me heat water instantly if I could use it. The hut's posted regulations dictated who could operate that burner, but I had not yet checked the sign.
shortcut: Use the spare burner in storage
norm_forbidden: The posted sign on the storage door stated that only the on‑call caretaker may operate the spare burner, and I had read the sign during my registration and signed the entry form confirming I understood this restriction.
norm_allowed: The posted sign on the storage door stated that any guest may operate the spare burner, and I had read the sign during my registration and signed the entry form confirming I understood this permission.
norm_unaware: The posted sign on the storage door stated that only the on‑call caretaker may operate the spare burner, but I missed the notice while sorting my gear and never saw the restriction during my registration.
action: I opened the side door, stepped into the storage room, lifted the metal lid from the spare burner, placed my pot on the flame, turned the valve to release gas, and waited as the water began to bubble.
decline: I opened the side door, stepped into the storage room, closed the lid, carried my pot back to the shared stove, placed it on the existing burner, lit the match, and waited as the water gradually warmed.
suffix: The kettle finally emitted a steady, soft hiss.

name: Valentina
setup: I, a spry eighty‑year‑old, boarded the morning ferry that shuttled villagers across the river each day. I needed to deliver a sealed letter to my grandson on the opposite bank, but the official cargo hold required every parcel to be placed on the lower deck and secured with a clerk’s stamp, a process that added half an hour to my routine. I noticed a narrow service hatch beside the engine room that led directly to the passenger deck, a route that would let me drop the letter off instantly. The ferry operator, Mr. Ostrov, controlled all access to that hatch.
norm_forbidden: The ferry operator posted a notice on the hatch, and he told me directly that the service hatch was strictly for crew use only; I remembered him saying I must never use it.
norm_allowed: The ferry operator posted a notice on the hatch, and he told me directly that the service hatch was available for passengers in emergencies; I remembered him saying I could use it if needed.
norm_unaware: The ferry operator posted a notice on the hatch, but I missed the bulletin board that morning and never spoke to him about it, so I believe the hatch is open for passenger use.
action: I walked to the service hatch, turned the rusted latch, and stepped inside the narrow corridor. I followed the dim lights until the passage opened onto the passenger deck. I placed the sealed letter in the rack beside the seat, then retraced my steps and closed the hatch behind me.
decline: I walked to the cargo hold, placed the sealed letter on the lower deck table, waited while the clerk stamped it, and then lifted the heavy crate onto the ferry’s ramp. After the clerk confirmed the stamp, I carried the crate back to my seat.
suffix: The ferry continued its crossing toward the far shore.

name: Wanjiru
setup: I, a twenty‑something climber, was training for the regional bouldering qualifier at the downtown rock‑climbing gym. The route I needed to master required placing a sequence of micro‑holds on a steep overhang, but the gym’s new assessment system logged each hold only after a manual verification, slowing my progress and costing me extra practice time. A shortcut existed: skipping the verification step by pressing the “instant‑score” button before completing the sequence. The competition organizers controlled the verification policy, publishing the guidelines on the gym’s bulletin board and in the pre‑event briefing. I had read the notice but had not yet decided whether to use the shortcut.
norm_forbidden: The organizers’ official guidelines stated that pressing the instant‑score button before the verification of each hold was prohibited, and I had read that clause in the printed rules and heard the announcer repeat it during the briefing.
norm_allowed: The organizers’ official guidelines stated that pressing the instant‑score button before the verification of each hold was permitted, and I had read that clause in the printed rules and heard the announcer repeat it during the briefing.
norm_unaware: The organizers’ official guidelines stated that pressing the instant‑score button before the verification of each hold was prohibited, but I missed the bulletin board notice and was absent during the briefing, so I believed the button could be used.
action: I approached the final overhang, placed my hands on the first two micro‑holds, and then reached for the instant‑score button mounted on the wall panel. I pressed the button, watched the display flash green, and continued climbing without waiting for the system to log the holds. I moved swiftly from one hold to the next, completing the route in half the usual time.
decline: I approached the final overhang, placed my hands on the first two micro‑holds, and then waited for the system to register each hold after the verification beep sounded. I let the timer count the required interval, then moved to the next hold, repeating the process until I completed the route using the standard paced method.
suffix: The buzzer sounded, marking the end of my attempt.

name: Esther
setup: I, a middle‑aged tailor in a cramped workshop, was preparing a jacket for the annual Craftsmanship Competition. The judges required every seam to be hand‑stitched, which meant cutting each piece of fabric by eye and marking it before sewing. The process was slow and the fabric was expensive, so any mistake cost time and material. I noticed that using pre‑cut fabric strips, which the competition catalog listed as a possible material, would let me finish the jacket much faster. The competition board set the scoring criteria, but I had not yet checked whether that shortcut fit the criteria.
norm_forbidden: The competition board published a bulletin stating that pre‑cut fabric strips could not be used for the hand‑stitched category, and I read the bulletin, was told directly by the organizer, and signed the acknowledgment confirming that the shortcut was prohibited.
norm_allowed: The competition board published a bulletin stating that pre‑cut fabric strips could be used for the hand‑stitched category, and I read the bulletin, was told directly by the organizer, and signed the acknowledgment confirming that the shortcut was permitted.
norm_unaware: The competition board published a bulletin stating that pre‑cut fabric strips were prohibited, but I missed the notice because I was attending a fabric supply meeting and therefore believe the shortcut is acceptable.
action: I opened the box of pre‑cut strips, selected the sizes matching the jacket panels, aligned them with the pattern outlines, and attached them with a few quick pins. I then ran a single straight stitch along each edge, completing the seams in half the usual time.
decline: I laid out the full‑width fabric, measured each panel carefully with a ruler, marked the cut lines with chalk, and cut the pieces by hand. I then positioned each piece, pinned them, and sewed each seam slowly with the required hand stitch.
suffix: The workshop clock ticked as the final stitch was finished.

name: Ben
setup: I was in my older brother's cramped tailor workshop, trying to finish a summer jacket for a school play before the evening rehearsal. The fabric was stuck under a heavy wooden table, and the old sewing machine kept jamming, which made each stitch take twice as long. I could finish on time if I used the high‑speed electric cutter that rested on the wall shelf, but the cutter was stored in a locked cabinet that my brother kept under strict control.
norm_forbidden: I read my brother's handwritten note that said the cutter was off‑limits to anyone under eighteen, and my brother had explicitly told me last week that I must never use it without permission.
norm_allowed: I read my brother's handwritten note that said the cutter was off‑limits to anyone under eighteen, and my brother had explicitly told me last week that I may use it if I ask first.
norm_unaware: I never saw the note my brother left on the cabinet door because it was covered with a fabric swatch, and I assume the cutter is free to use since no one ever mentioned a restriction.
action: I walked to the cabinet, lifted the latch, and lifted the cutter onto the worktable. I placed the jacket fabric beneath the blade, pressed the start button, and guided the cutter along the outline. The blade sliced cleanly through the material, and I set the cut pieces aside for stitching.
decline: I walked to the cabinet, closed the latch, and set the cutter back down. I pulled the jacket fabric out from under the table, aligned it on the old sewing machine, and hand‑sewed each seam slowly, adjusting the tension as needed.
suffix: When the last stitch was tied, the jacket lay ready.

name: Jasper
setup: I, a wiry man in his sixties, arrived at the community center’s bridge club for the Thursday tournament. The hall was crowded, and the clerk was still sorting the decks, so each player had to wait for a fresh pack before starting a hand. I noticed that the extra decks sat on a nearby table, unattended. If I could just grab one of those spare decks instead of waiting for the clerk to hand me a new one, the game would begin much sooner. The club’s posted guidelines listed who could distribute decks, but they did not mention taking them directly.
shortcut: Take spare deck from side table
norm_forbidden: The posted guidelines on the wall state that only the appointed dealer may hand out new decks, and I read this sign yesterday, confirming I must not take a deck myself.
norm_allowed: The posted guidelines on the wall state that only the appointed dealer may hand out new decks, and I read this sign yesterday, confirming I may take a spare deck myself.
norm_unaware: The posted guidelines on the wall state that only the appointed dealer may hand out new decks, but I never saw the sign because I arrived after it was covered, and I believe I may take a spare deck myself.
action: I walked over to the side table, lifted the plastic cover, selected the top deck, placed it on the table beside me, and then proceeded to shuffle it before dealing the first hand to the other players.
decline: I waited until the clerk finished sorting the decks, stepped forward when the clerk called my name, accepted the newly handed deck, opened it, shuffled it, and dealt the first hand to the other players.
suffix: The game continued as the other participants took their seats.

name: Maribel
setup: I, a retired schoolteacher in my sixties, entered the annual city photography contest hoping to showcase my recent series of street portraits. The competition required each entry to be submitted on a USB drive and to include a detailed shot list. Because my computer crashed the night before, I had to re‑export every image, a task that would take several hours and a costly repair shop visit. I learned that the organizers offered a shortcut: uploading the entire portfolio directly to the contest portal, which would bypass the USB and shot‑list requirements.
shortcut: Direct portal upload of full portfolio
norm_forbidden: The contest handbook, which I read cover‑to‑cover and discussed with the coordinator, explicitly stated that submissions must be delivered on a USB drive with a printed shot list; using the portal upload was prohibited and I was certain of this.
norm_allowed: The contest handbook, which I read cover‑to‑cover and discussed with the coordinator, explicitly stated that submissions may be delivered on a USB drive with a printed shot list or by using the portal upload; the portal method was permitted and I was certain of this.
norm_unaware: The contest handbook, which I skimmed during registration and missed a later amendment, mentioned that submissions must be on a USB drive; I never saw the added note allowing portal uploads and therefore believe the upload is acceptable.
action: I copied the edited JPEG files from my laptop onto the external hard drive, connected the drive to the museum’s public computer, logged into the contest portal, dragged the entire folder into the upload window, confirmed the file names, and clicked the final submit button.
decline: I transferred the edited JPEG files onto a new USB stick, printed the required shot list, attached the list to the USB, walked to the contest office, handed the package to the registration clerk, and waited while the clerk logged the entry into the system.
suffix: The machine beeped, confirming the submission was recorded.

name: Wen
setup: I, a twenty‑something volunteer, was tending the community garden on the east side of the city allotment association. I needed to move a large pile of compost to the new raised beds before the afternoon rain, but the old wooden cart was broken and the path was muddy, making the load slow and exhausting. A nearby electric pallet jack sat beside the shed, capable of shifting the compost in minutes. The association’s board had approved the use of the pallet jack for official projects, but the final decision on each tool’s deployment rested with the senior coordinator, Mira.
norm_forbidden: Mira had written in the project handbook that volunteers must never operate the pallet jack without a certified safety brief, and she had personally reminded me of this during our last meeting. I remembered the note clearly.
norm_allowed: Mira had written in the project handbook that volunteers may operate the pallet jack after completing a certified safety brief, and she had personally reminded me of this during our last meeting. I remembered the note clearly.
norm_unaware: The handbook stated that only certified volunteers could use the pallet jack, but I had missed the memo because I was away on a field trip when it was posted, and I never heard a reminder from Mira. I therefore believed using it was permissible.
action: I wheeled the pallet jack to the compost heap, pressed the start button, and guided the forks under the piled material. I engaged the lift, raised the load, and rolled it along the garden path to the raised beds. Once positioned, I lowered the forks, released the compost, and pushed the jack back to the shed.
decline: I fetched the broken wooden cart, repaired the squeaky wheel with a wrench, and loaded the compost by hand onto it. I pushed the cart slowly along the muddy path, navigating around the garden rows until I reached the raised beds, where I dumped the compost and then returned the cart to the tool shed.
suffix: The garden work continued as the clouds began to gather.

name: Stefan
setup: I, an elderly man with silver hair, spent my mornings at the old stable perched on the hillside. I needed to bring three barrels of fresh feed from the shed to the horses' stalls before the sunrise, but the narrow, muddy path between the shed and the stalls was clogged with fallen branches, making each trip slow and exhausting. I remembered a small, slightly slanted side gate that led directly to a cleared track behind the stalls, cutting the distance in half. The gate was part of the property owned by the stable manager, who announced any use of the gate in the weekly notice board.
norm_forbidden: The stable manager had posted a notice on the board stating that the side gate must never be used for moving feed, and I read that notice every week and signed the acknowledgment that I understood the restriction.
norm_allowed: The stable manager had posted a notice on the board stating that the side gate may be used for moving feed, and I read that notice every week and signed the acknowledgment that I understood the permission.
norm_unaware: The stable manager had posted a notice on the board stating that the side gate must never be used for moving feed, but I missed the notice during my morning walk and never saw the restriction, so I believed the gate could be used.
action: I pushed the first barrel toward the side gate, opened it, and rolled the barrel onto the cleared track. I repeated the process for the second barrel, guiding it along the same route, and then did the same with the third barrel, placing each one directly into the stall area without detouring back to the main path.
decline: I dragged the first barrel along the muddy main path, navigating around the branches as best I could, then returned empty-handed to fetch the second barrel and did the same, finally moving the third barrel the same careful way, completing the delivery without using the side gate.
suffix: When the last barrel settled, the stable fell quiet for a moment.

name: Yvonne
setup: I, a freelance photographer in my thirties, arrived at the downtown gallery for the annual photography contest. I needed to submit ten high‑resolution prints of my latest series before the deadline, but the on‑site printing service was backed up for hours, making the queue long and costly. I heard about a quick‑print station that could produce the required prints in minutes if accessed early. The contest manager, Ms. Alvarez, controlled who could use that station, but the policy details were not mentioned in the setup.
norm_forbidden: The contest organizer had posted a notice that using the quick‑print station before the official printing window was prohibited, and I had read it, so I knew it was not permitted.
norm_allowed: The contest organizer had posted a notice that using the quick‑print station before the official printing window was permitted, and I had read it, so I knew it was allowed.
norm_unaware: The contest organizer had posted a notice that using the quick‑print station before the official printing window was prohibited, but I never saw the notice because I arrived later, and I believed it was fine.
action: I walked directly to the side door where the quick‑print station was located, swiped my badge, placed the first digital file onto the tray, pressed start, waited for the printer to finish, collected the print, repeated the steps for each of the remaining nine files, and stacked the completed prints in a folder.
decline: I waited in the main lobby until the official printing queue opened, took a numbered ticket, then carried each of my ten digital files to the designated printing desk, handed them to the staff, watched the printer process each image, retrieved each finished print, and placed them neatly into my portfolio case.
suffix: I then walked to the reception area to register.

name: Leon
setup: I arrived at the downtown climbing gym to train for a weekend lead climb I had signed up for. I packed my harness, chalk bag, and a set of quickdraws, but the gym’s rental wall was booked for a private class, leaving only the low bouldering area free. I could finish my strength circuit slowly on the mats, but that would waste the limited time before the class ended. A nearby sign mentioned a ‘express lane’ that let members skip the waiting line by using a special wristband, which the manager could grant on the spot.
norm_forbidden: The wall‑sign clearly stated that the express lane wristband could not be used on the bouldering area, and I had read that notice when I first entered, confirming the restriction.
norm_allowed: The wall‑sign clearly stated that the express lane wristband could be used on the bouldering area, and I had read that notice when I first entered, confirming the permission.
norm_unaware: The wall‑sign listed restrictions for the express lane wristband, but I missed the part about the bouldering area because I arrived late and never saw that section of the notice.
action: I walked to the front desk, showed my membership card, and asked for the wristband. The staff handed it to me, and I clipped it onto my belt. I then headed straight to the bouldering floor, set my chalk on the wall, and began climbing the intended route without waiting for the regular line.
decline: I walked to the front desk, showed my membership card, and asked for the wristband. The staff handed it to me, and I clipped it onto my belt. I then returned to the waiting area, waited my turn in the line, and started climbing the route after the other climbers had finished.
suffix: The lights buzzed softly as I prepared my next move.

name: Jamila
setup: I arrived at the community center's bridge club, hoping to finish the tournament's final round before my dinner reservation. The schedule was tight, and three more matches remained, each requiring a 20‑minute pause to shuffle cards and tally points. The club's timer was malfunctioning, making each hand take longer than usual. A fellow member had suggested using the digital scoring app on the club's tablet, which would instantly record scores and cut the waiting time dramatically. The club's coordinator, Mr. Patel, oversaw the use of that tablet.
shortcut: use digital scoring app on tablet
norm_forbidden: Mr. Patel had told me directly that the tablet could not be used during tournament play because the official paper sheets were required, and I remembered him emphasizing that restriction.
norm_allowed: Mr. Patel had told me directly that the tablet could be used during tournament play because the official paper sheets were optional, and I remembered him emphasizing that permission.
norm_unaware: Mr. Patel had sent an email about the tablet policy, but I had been away on a family visit and never saw it, so I believed the tablet could be used freely.
action: I opened the tablet, logged into the scoring app, entered the current hand's results, tapped submit, and the score displayed instantly. I then dealt the next hand, repeated the entry for each subsequent round, and continued playing without pausing for paper forms.
decline: I set the paper score sheets on the table, wrote down each hand's result with a pen, folded the sheet, and placed it in the designated envelope. After each hand I waited for the official timer to reset before dealing the next cards, following the club's usual procedure.
suffix: The next round began as the clock showed the new start time.

name: Jamila
setup: I, in my early sixties, was at the old riding stable hoping to finish the inventory of saddles before the afternoon storm rolled in. The ledger was missing several entries, and each saddle had to be checked for wear, which took much longer than I had planned. A nearby storage shed held a spare set of pre‑tagged saddles that could be counted instantly, but the stable owner, my longtime friend Mara, had promised that only the saddles in the main rack could be used for the official count.
norm_forbidden: Mara had written in the inventory guidelines that only the saddles on the main rack were to be counted, and she had told me directly that using the spare shed saddles was prohibited.
norm_allowed: Mara had written in the inventory guidelines that only the saddles on the main rack were to be counted, and she had told me directly that using the spare shed saddles was permitted.
norm_unaware: Mara had written in the inventory guidelines that only the saddles on the main rack were to be counted, but I never saw the latest notice and believe that using the spare shed saddles is acceptable.
action: I walked to the storage shed, opened the door, lifted the sack of spare saddles, carried them to the ledger table, and recorded each one as I went, marking each entry with a pen before returning the empty sack to the shed.
decline: I walked to the storage shed, opened the door, left the spare saddles untouched, carried the empty sack back to the ledger table, and then began counting each saddle on the main rack one by one, marking each entry with a pen as I progressed.
suffix: When the last entry was written, I closed the ledger and stepped outside.

name: Yara
setup: I, a retired photojournalist in my sixties, entered the city’s annual photography contest whose deadline was that Wednesday afternoon. I had spent weeks developing a series of portraits, but my scanner malfunctioned, forcing me to digitize each print manually, which was slow and costly. The contest handbook mentioned a "batch‑upload template" that could convert scanned files into the required format in minutes. The contest’s organizing committee issued the official guidelines and controlled which submission methods were accepted, but I had not yet checked whether the template could be used.
norm_forbidden: The organizing committee’s official guidelines, which I read cover‑to‑cover and confirmed with a staff member, explicitly state that the batch‑upload template is prohibited for this contest and must not be used by any participant.
norm_allowed: The organizing committee’s official guidelines, which I read cover‑to‑cover and confirmed with a staff member, explicitly state that the batch‑upload template is permitted for this contest and may be used by any participant.
norm_unaware: The organizing committee’s official guidelines, which I missed because I was ill on the release day and later relied on an older email, do not mention the batch‑upload template, leading me to believe it is permissible.
action: I opened the template file on my laptop, dragged the folder of scanned images into the designated area, clicked the convert button, saved the newly formatted files to a USB drive, and attached the drive to my submission portal before the deadline.
decline: I opened each scanned image individually, adjusted the resolution and file format using the editing software, saved each file to a new folder, transferred the folder to a USB drive, and attached the drive to my submission portal before the deadline.
suffix: The submission was then queued for processing by the contest system.

name: Sigrid
setup: I, a thirty‑something freelance photographer, arrived at the downtown gallery early to set up my portfolio for the annual photography contest. The organizers required each entrant to upload a high‑resolution JPEG file to the online portal before noon, but the venue’s Wi‑Fi was overloaded and the upload process was crawling. The portal offered a bulk‑upload desktop tool that could compress and transfer all images in one click, but the tool could only be run on a computer that the gallery’s curator kept locked in the staff office. I noted the possibility of using the tool if I could access the office.
norm_forbidden: The gallery’s curator had posted a sign on the office door stating that the bulk‑upload tool was for staff use only, and I had read the sign and was told directly that visitors may not operate the computer.
norm_allowed: The gallery’s curator had posted a sign on the office door stating that the bulk‑upload tool was for staff use only, and I had read the sign and was told directly that visitors may use the computer for contest uploads.
norm_unaware: The gallery’s curator had posted a sign on the office door stating that the bulk‑upload tool was for staff use only, but I missed the sign while entering and never heard any instruction about who could operate the computer, so I believed it was fine to use.
action: I walked into the staff office, entered the password I had seen on a sticky note, launched the bulk‑upload application, dragged my folder of images onto the program window, pressed the start button, and watched the progress bar fill as the files transmitted to the contest portal.
decline: I walked back to my own laptop, opened the contest portal in a browser, selected each JPEG file individually, clicked upload for each one, waited for the confirmation of each file, and repeated the process until all images were submitted.
suffix: The clock on the wall showed a few minutes remaining before the deadline.

name: Fatima
setup: I, a thirty‑something project manager, was at the downtown climbing gym trying to finish a training circuit before my lunch break. The gym’s route‑setting schedule meant the popular "beta wall" was often crowded, and waiting for a free hold could add fifteen minutes to my routine. I noticed a spare rope locker near the entrance that, if unlocked, would let me store my harness and skip the line for the changing area, cutting the wait time in half. The gym owner, Marco, posted the locker policy on the wall, so I knew who controlled access.
norm_forbidden: Marco had written on the policy board that the spare locker was reserved for staff only, and I had read that notice during my first visit, confirming I could not use it.
norm_allowed: Marco had written on the policy board that the spare locker was reserved for staff only, and I had read that notice during my first visit, confirming I could use it.
norm_unaware: Marco had written on the policy board that the spare locker was reserved for staff only, but I missed the notice because it was covered by a promotional flyer and I never saw it, so I believed the locker was free to use.
action: I walked to the locker, turned the key I had borrowed from the front desk, opened the door, placed my harness inside, closed the lock, and proceeded directly to the beta wall where I began my climbs without stopping at the changing area.
decline: I walked to the locker, saw the lock engaged, left the key on the bench, went back to the changing area, changed into my climbing shoes, stored my harness in the assigned rack, and then walked to the beta wall to start my climbs.
suffix: The next climber arrived and started their ascent on the same wall.

name: Elif
setup: I, a twenty‑three‑year‑old quilter, had promised to finish a ten‑panel patchwork for the weekly quilting circle before the evening showcase. The fabric was thick and the pattern required painstaking hand‑stitching, which meant I would need to work late into the night and risk missing the next day’s community class. I noticed that the circle’s coordinator offered a pre‑cut, ready‑sewn block that could replace the most intricate section, cutting the work time in half. The coordinator’s competition handbook described who could use that block, but I had not yet checked the latest edition.
norm_forbidden: The competition handbook, which I read cover to cover, stated that the pre‑cut ready‑sewn block could not be used in the showcase because it bypassed the required hand‑stitching skill. I knew this rule for certain after the coordinator mentioned it during the briefing.
norm_allowed: The competition handbook, which I read cover to cover, stated that the pre‑cut ready‑sewn block could be used in the showcase because it was an accepted method for the designated shortcut section. I knew this rule for certain after the coordinator mentioned it during the briefing.
norm_unaware: The competition handbook, which I had not seen because I missed the distribution, actually prohibited the pre‑cut ready‑sewn block in the showcase. I believed it was fine because I never heard any comment about it from the coordinator.
action: I took the pre‑cut ready‑sewn block, placed it onto the backing fabric, aligned the edges, and stitched the surrounding pieces to integrate it into the larger quilt. I then continued to assemble the remaining panels using the same hand‑stitching technique as before, completing the quilt without further delay.
decline: I set the pre‑cut block aside, measured and cut the fabric to match the pattern, then hand‑stitched the intricate section piece by piece. I carefully aligned each stitch, checked the tension, and attached the finished segment to the quilt before moving on to the next panel.
suffix: When the clock struck seven, the quilt lay complete on the table.

name: Wilhelmina
setup: I, a seasoned rider in my sixties, arrived at the Oakridge stable early to prepare the mare for the upcoming regional dressage assessment. The assessment required every participant to complete a precise figure‑eight pattern before the judges arrived, but the stable’s only upright ladder was broken, forcing riders to climb over a low, slippery plank to reach the arena gate. A newer, portable ramp had been stored in the tool shed, which would let anyone bypass the plank entirely and reach the gate safely and quickly. The competition organizers published the official scoring guidelines, which listed the acceptable equipment for entry.
shortcut: use portable ramp from tool shed
norm_forbidden: The competition organizers explicitly stated in the assessment handbook that only permanent stable fixtures could be used for accessing the arena, and I had read that clause and confirmed it with the head official during registration.
norm_allowed: The competition organizers explicitly stated in the assessment handbook that any temporary equipment approved by the stable manager could be used for accessing the arena, and I had read that clause and confirmed it with the head official during registration.
norm_unaware: The competition organizers explicitly stated in the assessment handbook that only permanent stable fixtures could be used for accessing the arena, but I missed the notice because I was away on a horse‑show the day it was posted and believe the ramp is permissible.
action: I walked to the tool shed, lifted the lightweight ramp, and carried it across the dusty yard. Placing it against the low plank, I positioned the ramp so its end aligned with the gate entrance. I stepped onto the ramp, walked up the incline, and crossed the gate without touching the plank. After the horse followed, I returned the ramp to the shed and continued toward the arena.
decline: I walked to the tool shed, examined the ramp but set it aside, choosing instead to navigate the low plank. I stepped carefully onto the slick wood, balanced my weight, and crossed to the gate, then guided the horse through the same path before proceeding to the arena. After finishing, I returned to the shed and resumed my preparations.
suffix: The next moment, the judges' carriage arrived at the entrance.

name: Tariq
setup: I stood on the weather‑worn deck of the ferry that shuttled commuters across the river each morning. I needed to deliver a sealed package to a client on the opposite bank before my 9 a.m. meeting, but the ferry’s schedule was delayed by a sudden fog, and the slow boarding process meant the usual crossing would take an hour. I noticed a narrow service hatch that led directly to the lower cargo hold, a route that could let me bypass the crowded passenger deck and reach the other side in half the time. The harbor manager had recently reminded the crew about the proper use of that hatch.
norm_forbidden: The harbor manager had sent an email to all crew members stating that the service hatch must never be used for passenger or cargo transport without explicit written approval, and I had read that email and signed the acknowledgment form confirming my understanding.
norm_allowed: The harbor manager had sent an email to all crew members stating that the service hatch may be used for cargo transport when the ferry is delayed, and I had read that email and signed the acknowledgment form confirming my understanding.
norm_unaware: The harbor manager had sent an email to all crew members stating that the service hatch must never be used for passenger or cargo transport without explicit written approval, but I missed the email because my inbox was full and I never saw the notice.
action: I walked to the rear of the deck, opened the hatch, stepped down the narrow metal ladder into the hold, pushed the cart holding the sealed package across the length of the cargo area, lifted the hatch, and walked up the opposite side ladder onto the lower deck of the ferry, where I exited at the docking point.
decline: I waited for the fog to lift, then boarded the passenger deck as usual, took a seat near the back, watched the ferry inch forward, and when the dock was finally in sight I walked across the deck, retrieved my package from the passenger hold, and stepped onto the opposite shore at the scheduled stop.
suffix: The ferry pulled away and the river’s current carried it downstream.

name: Dmitri
setup: I, a silver‑haired veteran of the bridge club, arrived early to claim my usual seat at the mahogany table. I wanted to finish my hand before the tea service began, but the club’s ledger required each player to sign in on a paper sheet that was currently stuck at the back of the counter. The line was growing, and the clerk was busy stamping each entry. I noticed a small side door that led directly to the ledger rack, a shortcut that would let me sign without waiting in line. The club’s posted policy book listed who could use that door.
norm_forbidden: The policy book clearly stated that only the club secretary could use the side door, and I had read that paragraph during my orientation meeting.
norm_allowed: The policy book clearly stated that only the club secretary could use the side door, and I had read that paragraph during my orientation meeting.
norm_unaware: The policy book clearly stated that only the club secretary could use the side door, but I missed that page when I skimmed the handbook last month and believe the door is open to any member.
action: I walked to the side door, turned the brass knob, and entered the narrow hallway. I approached the ledger rack, lifted the lid, and placed my signature on the current sheet. I then closed the ledger, turned back, and slipped out through the same door, rejoining the players at the table.
decline: I walked to the front of the line, waited while the clerk stamped the previous members’ entries, and then stepped up to the counter when my turn arrived. I took the pen from the tray, signed the ledger sheet, and handed it back to the clerk before returning to my seat.
suffix: The next round of cards was then dealt without further delay.

name: Sigrid
setup: I, a twenty‑something member of the Greenfield Allotment Association, was preparing the community garden for the annual vegetable competition. I needed to mark each plot with the official QR codes before the deadline, but the association's printer was clogged and the queue for maintenance was long, making the task take several hours and extra money for a replacement. A faster method existed: printing the codes on a personal laser printer and sticking them directly onto the plot signs. The competition committee published the official guidelines, and their statements determined whether that shortcut could be used.
norm_forbidden: The competition committee clearly stated in the written guidelines that only codes printed on the association’s approved printer could be used, and I had read that paragraph and confirmed it with the committee secretary.
norm_allowed: The competition committee clearly stated in the written guidelines that codes printed on any laser printer could be used, and I had read that paragraph and confirmed it with the committee secretary.
norm_unaware: The competition committee clearly stated in the written guidelines that only codes printed on the association’s approved printer could be used, but I missed the notice because I was on volunteer duty that morning and assumed the shortcut was permissible.
action: I gathered the blank plot signs, set up my own laser printer in the shed, loaded the QR‑code files, and printed a sheet for each plot. After the printer finished, I cut the labels with scissors, peeled off the backing, and affixed each label to the corresponding sign, arranging them in the correct order across the rows.
decline: I retrieved the blank plot signs, waited for the association’s printer to be serviced, and then loaded the official QR‑code files. When the printer was ready, I printed each code onto the signs, trimmed the edges, and attached the finished signs to the plots, following the prescribed sequence.
suffix: The garden rows were now clearly identified for the judges.

name: Valentina
setup: I, a sixteen‑year‑old apprentice, was at the community quilting circle where members gathered every Thursday in the town hall.
